L1514: The Applicant provided an external, blinded, review of the serious AESIs of gastric or esophageal erosions from ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND. This review found that most included events were overt gastrointestinal bleeding, with over half requiring transfusion. However, the external blinded review also noted several limitations related to the fact that the AE reports did not trigger confirmatory testing (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori* testing and confirmatory endoscopy).
L1515: As a potential risk mitigation strategy, we considered known risk factors which were also reported in the subject level dataset. These included smoking history, use of aspirin, clopidogrel, and vitamin K antagonists (e.g., warfarin) at baseline. In the pooled ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND dataset, aspirin was independently associated with serious gastrointestinal erosions/bleeds (HR 1.52 [95% CI: 1.1 – 2.1]), as was clopidogrel (HR 1.16 [95% CI: 0.7 – 1.9]), and warfarin (HR 2.0 [95% CI: 1.1 – 3.4]). Smoking history was not strongly related.
L1516: Subgroup analyses for serious gastric erosions/bleeds did not suggest a substantial treatment interaction with concomitant aspirin, warfarin, or clopidogrel (Table 105). It is important to note that the warfarin and clopidogrel subgroups were limited in the trial population (less than 10% of subjects used warfarin or clopidogrel). Approximately one-half used aspirin. These products (as well as others, such as NSAIDs) may increase the risk of GI bleeding. The data from ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND are too limited to reliably assess the extent of the role these agents played in the GI bleeding risk with daprodustat.

L1528: ## Conclusion
L1529: In summary, there was a treatment difference in serious esophageal and gastric erosions disfavoring daprodustat that was more pronounced in ASCEND-ND than ASCEND-D. Whether there is a true risk in the ASCEND-D population is unclear as there are some inconsistencies in the data. For example, all TEAEs of esophageal and gastric erosions (serious plus non-serious) did not disfavor daprodustat in ASCEND-D. Also, the risk of serious esophageal and gastric erosions in the on-study analysis of ASCEND-D was not apparent or became weaker in the OT analyses. Other limitations include the lack of confirmatory testing, including endoscopy. Nonetheless, most of these reported serious events were related to gastrointestinal bleeding and had important clinical consequences such as transfusions and at this time we cannot rule out a drug effect based on the nonclinical findings and signal in both ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND populations. Therefore, we will include a Warning and Precaution in the label, recommending the healthcare provider consider this risk, particularly in patients who have risk factors for erosions.
L1530: ## 7.7.8. Acute Kidney Injury
L1531: ## Issue
L1532: A higher incidence of serious investigator reported treatment emergent AEs related to AKI was observed in the daprodustat arm compared to the ESA comparator arm in ASCEND-ND.
L1533: ## Background
L1534: Direct daprodustat-mediated nephrotoxicity was not observed in the nonclinical program (although there were effects secondary to non-physiologic Hb levels and blood viscosity, leading to compromised blood flow and vascular perfusion, including in the kidney). In ASCEND-ND, the time to first occurrence of CKD progression was a pre-specified principal secondary endpoint, which was assessed in participants with preserved kidney function at baseline (eGFR \ge 15 mL/min/1.73 m^2, N=2,485). This endpoint was a composite of a confirmed (through repeat eGFR) 40% decline in eGFR, clinical indication for dialysis, transition to chronic dialysis, or receipt of a renal allograft. CKD progression was generally similar between the treatment groups and daprodustat did not significantly reduce the time to progression of CKD compared with darbepoetin (IRD [95% CI] -0.2 [-2.8, 2.4] events per 100 PY, HR 0.98, 95% CI: 0.84, 1.13). Routine safety laboratory results (collected at least every 12 weeks) in ASCEND-ND (e.g., aggregate longitudinal plots and shift tables) for serum creatinine, eGFR, and BUN was similar between treatment groups.
L1535: In contrast, the FDA analyses using treatment-emergent serious adverse events (TESAEs) of AKI shows a potential increased risk for serious AKI for daprodustat compared to the ESA treatment arm in the NDD population.
L1536: ## Assessment
L1537: We performed exploratory analyses to further refine the safety signal of AKI. Adverse event analyses of serious AKI (as a nFMQ) in ASCEND-ND showed a relative risk of 1.47 (95% CI 1.07, 2.00) and risk difference of 1.54% [0.30, 2.79]). The risks were attenuated when considering all AKI TEAEs regardless of seriousness (relative risk of 1.2, 95% CI [-0.4, 2.7]). We note that the treatment difference appears after 16 months on study, so we preferred cumulative incidence differences to quantify risk. A Kaplan-Meier curve for time to first treatment-emergent serious adverse event (TESAE) of AKI for the ASCEND-ND study is presented in Figure 36. At 2 and 3 years, there was a cumulative incidence difference of 2.1% (95% CI: 0.5, 3.5) and 2.7% (95% CI 0.8, 4.6), respectively.
L1538: **Figure 36. Time to First TESAE of Acute Kidney Injury (Narrow FMQ) in ASCEND-ND, (On-Study Analysis)**
L1539: Source: Clinical Reviewer, ADAE.xpt, ADSL.xpt, R v. 4.2, ITT population; TESAEs of acute kidney injury (narrow) per FMQ v. 2.0. This analysis treats deaths and administrative censoring the same.
Abbreviations: Dapro, daprodustat; ESA, erythropoietin-stimulating agent; FMQ, FDA medical query; ITT, intent-to-treat; TESAE, treatment-emergent serious adverse event
L1540: There was a higher percentage of participants randomized to the daprodustat arm with more progressed CKD (i.e., stage 4 or 5), and advanced age (\ge 75-year-old age), which may have contributed, to some degree, to the observed treatment difference (both are risk factors for AKI). However, an analysis provided by the Applicant, adjusting for baseline CKD stage, did not meaningfully change the estimate of harm (Table 46 of advisory committee briefing document).
L1541: The Applicant's key secondary endpoint, by design, does not capture acute AKI events, because a repeat measurement of eGFR was required to confirm a 40% decline in eGFR. A sensitivity analysis, which included a single measurement of a 40% decline in eGFR as a CKD progression event, did capture an unfavorable treatment difference. Lastly, the occurrence of a serious event is clinically important, regardless of whether it contributed to long term outcomes (such as progression of CKD or ACM). We acknowledge that the predefined adjudicated secondary safety analyses such as ACM (HR 1.03, 95% CI: 0.87, 1.20) and CKD progression (HR 0.98, 95% CI: 0.84, 1.13) were balanced between arms.
L1542: We considered whether the AKI TESAE imbalance could be related to the increased risk for HHF with daprodustat compared to darbepoetin alfa. However, the AKI risk was still evident in
L1543: subjects without a history of heart failure at baseline (data not shown); a population that did not appear to have an increased risk of HHF with daprodustat compared to darbepoetin alfa.
L1544: Most patients with TESAE AKI events recovered, with most events lasting 14 to 16 days. Most events occurred while receiving study drug (16 to 19% occurred off treatment) (see Table 107).

L1549: ## Conclusion
L1550: In summary, there are discrepant lines of evidence regarding kidney injury with daprodustat in the NDD population. There were no differences detected for all-cause mortality or CKD progression, which are important sequelae of AKI. Since this risk is specific to the NDD population, risk mitigation strategies are premature for our planned DD-only approval (b) (4)
L1551: ## 7.7.9. Malignancy
L1552: ## Issue
L1553: Tumor progression, recurrence, and cancer-related mortality are theoretical risks based on the hypoxia-inducible factor biology.
L1554: ## Background
L1555: Hypoxia inducible factors are transcription factors involved in the hypoxia response and impact the expression of a number of survival genes in cancer cells and the tumor microenvironment. Daprodustat increases erythropoietin as part of its mechanism of action and drug labels for
L1556: marketed erythropoiesis stimulating agents include an increased risk of tumor progression as a boxed warning. Whether daprodustat shares this risk of ESA products is uncertain.
L1557: Lifetime studies in rodents did not identify a carcinogenic effect of daprodustat. However, based on the findings with ESAs and the theoretical risk related to the mechanism of action of daprodustat, the Applicant prespecified malignancy as an AESI. The Applicant's prespecified analysis approach for non-CV events was OT, defined by the last dose given plus 1 day. The ITT/on study analysis is more sensitive than the OT for long-latency events (such as malignancy), and less confounded by differences in dosing frequency (such as the darbepoetin alfa comparator in ASCEND-ND)(see Section 7.6.1.1.2).
L1558: The ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND protocols required treatment discontinuation following a diagnosis of cancer (new or recurrent), with the exception of squamous cell or basal cell carcinoma of the skin. Therefore, in the on-treatment assessment a malignancy diagnosis that was made two or more days after the last dose was not counted as an event, because per-protocol, subjects would not be dosed again. This scenario would be expected to exclude more events occurring with a drug dosed less frequently, but that are still very proximal to randomized treatment.
L1559: ## Assessment
L1560: For the above reasons, we considered the OT analysis as prespecified in the protocol but focused mainly on the on-study estimates for assessment of malignancy risk. We used a pooled analysis of ASCEND-ND and ASCEND-D and included treatment-emergent events regardless of reported seriousness. A summary of these results is presented in Table 108.
L1561: The on-study analysis did not suggest a treatment group difference in the incidence of malignancy (152 of 3419 [4.4%] daprodustat and 161 of 3407 [4.7%] ESA control with a relative risk of 0.9 (95% CI 0.8, 1.2). There did not appear to be notable imbalances in any pattern type or location of cancer between treatment groups. Fatal outcomes due to malignancy in both arms were infrequent.

L1569: Estimates of harm specific to the dialysis dependent population are required for the purposes of product labeling. Serious and nonserious malignancies (prespecified AESI query) were observed in 4.4% (n=65,) in ASCEND-D treated with daprodustat and 5.2% (n = 77,) of patients treated with rhEPO. Related queries (i.e., narrow FMQ, narrow SMQ for Malignancy) estimated similar incidences and treatment differences. The clinical reviewer reproduced the Applicant's estimated incidence rates for each treatment arm (1.9 per 100 PY for daprodustat, and 2.3 per 100 PY for subjects treated with ESA), using the submitted time-to-event datasets (adtte3.xpt).
L1570: ## Conclusion
L1571: In summary, the risk for tumor progression does not appear to be further increased compared to currently labeled ESAs, however, the short latency period of the studies conducted to date and the low event rates for specific cancers do not allow for definite conclusions on the long-term risk of daprodustat on tumor progression or development of new malignancies. For this reason, we are requiring a post-marketing observational study to access long term outcomes of daprodustat on malignancy incidence. In addition, a risk for malignancy will be included in the warnings and precautions section of the label. Refer to the postmarketing requirement (PMR) in Section 24 for additional details.
L1572: ## 7.7.10. Drug Induced Liver Injury
L1573: ## Issue
L1574: We assessed if there was a clinically significant hepatocellular injury risk with the use of daprodustat in subjects with CKD.
L1575: ## Background
L1576: There was no significant hepatotoxicity signal identified by the Applicant during development of daprodustat. Early during our exploratory review of individual patient data, an imbalance of potential Hy's law cases, not favoring daprodustat, was observed in routinely collected study site labs (pooled ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND: 4/3424 cases in the daprodustat arm, 2/3412 cases in the ESA comparator arm). Inspection of mean-level hepatic injury biomarkers versus time (aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, bilirubin) as well as shift tables did not reveal a population-wide signal. However, out of an abundance of caution, we consulted the Drug Induced Liver Injury (DILI) team to assess whether there is a DILI risk with daprodustat (Refer to DILI review dated November 29, 2022 in DARRTs).
L1577: ## Assessment
L1578: Our initial exploratory DILI analysis only included routine, study-site laboratory data. Per protocol, non-study site lab data was missing from the integrated laboratory dataset (i.e., the ADLB.xpt dataset). On August 5, 2022, the Applicant submitted an updated ADLB dataset for each ASCEND study and the Integrated Summary of Safety including central and non-study site lab results (importantly, the Applicant conducted a manual search in case report forms to locate non-study site data and update the ADLB dataset, as requested). For all Integrated Summary of Safety subjects, there were no clear imbalances in incidence of alanine aminotransferase/ aspartate aminotransferase elevations, jaundice, or cases meeting Hy's Law liver test criteria between subjects receiving daprodustat versus those receiving rhEPO (Table 109).

Only one was considered possible with alcohol as a competing cause.
L1584: ## Conclusion
L1585: The NDA data for daprodustat do not identify a significant liver injury risk that would preclude a favorable benefit-risk assessment. However, there were issues regarding missing data (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) that may have impaired a more thorough evaluation. The DILI team recommends labeling to monitor liver enzymes and bilirubin at baseline and as clinically indicated and recommends including liver injury in a post market pharmacovigilance strategy.
L1586: ## 7.8. Risk and Evaluation Mitigation Strategy
L1587: The Division of Risk Management (DRM) and Office of Medication Error Prevention and Risk Management (OMEPRM) were consulted. The conclusions from their review are summarized below.
L1588: Based on the available data, a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy is not necessary to ensure the benefits of daprodustat in the DD population outweigh the risks. The safety concerns associated with daprodustat use are similar to ESAs including the risk of MACE and healthcare providers who treat anemia of CKD are familiar with and able to appropriately monitor these risks.
L1589: If an Applicant resubmits daprodustat for use in the NDD population, a re-evaluation of the need for a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy will be conducted at that time.
L1590: For additional details, refer to the review by Carla Darling, PharmD, BCPS, Jacqueline Sheppard, Pharm D and Cynthia LaCivita, Pharm D, dated January 26, 2023 in DARRTs.
L1591: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L1592: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L1593: ## Hepatic Impairment
L1594: The Applicant did not propose any dose modifications for patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment. Patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh C) were not studied, and the Applicant recommends that treatment with daprodustat be avoided in that population.
L1595: ## Mild and Moderate Hepatic Impairment
L1596: A dedicated hepatic impairment study (Study 200231) was conducted where participants with mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class A (Score 5 to 6)), moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B (Score 7 to 9)) and their matched healthy controls with normal hepatic function were administered a single 6 mg oral dose of daprodustat in a fasted state. Results are shown below in Table 110.
L1597: Daprodustat C_{max} and AUC geometric least square mean ratios [90% CI] were 1.9-fold [1.06, 3.71] and 2.0-fold [1.10, 3.61] higher, respectively, in subjects with moderate hepatic impairment (Cohort 1) compared with their matched healthy control subjects (Cohort 2). All metabolites exposure geometric least square mean ratios were between 1.2-fold and 1.7-fold
L1598: higher in subjects with moderate hepatic impairment (Cohort 1) compared with their matched healthy control subjects (Cohort 2).
L1599: C_{max} for daprodustat was similar between subjects with mild hepatic impairment (Cohort 3) and their matched healthy controls (Cohort 4). The C_{max} geometric least square mean ratio [90% CI] was 1.01 [0.71, 1.43]. The daprodustat AUC geometric least square mean ratio [90% CI] was 1.46-fold [1.03, 2.05] higher in subjects with mild hepatic impairment compared with their matched healthy control subjects. C_{max} and AUC geometric least square mean ratios for all metabolites were between 1.3-fold and 2.0-fold higher in subjects with mild hepatic impairment compared with their matched healthy control subjects.
L1600: Daprodustat is highly protein bound. The fraction unbound (f_u) in the 3-hour post-dose plasma samples was 0.0034 in the participants with moderate hepatic impairment and 0.0028 in their matched healthy controls. Unbound AUC and C_{max} of daprodustat were 2.2-fold to 2.3-fold higher in subjects with moderate and mild hepatic impairment compared to their matched healthy cohorts. However, high variability (33.2–578% CV) was noted for the unbound PK parameters. In general, time to maximum concentration (T_{max}, median ~1.5 hours for daprodustat and 3 to 4 hours for the metabolites) and the t_{1/2} (mean ~4 to 4.5 h for daprodustat and 2.7 to 5.6 h for the metabolites) was similar across Cohorts 1 to 4.

L1612: Cohort 1 = Moderate hepatic impairment, Cohort 2 = Matched healthy controls for moderate hepatic impairment, Cohort 3 = Mild hepatic impairment, Cohort 4 = Matched healthy controls for mild hepatic impairment
L1613: Daprodustat is titrated to attain and maintain a target hemoglobin level of 11 g/dL. It is important to prevent a rapid increase in Hb or attaining too high a Hb level (&gt;11 g/dL) in patients with CKD as rapid or excessive Hb increases have been associated with the risk of severe adverse cardiovascular events and death in patients treated with ESAs, another treatment for anemia of CKD. A 2-fold increase in exposure of daprodustat in patients with moderate hepatic impairment may be associated with too large an increase in Hb. Therefore, a reduction of the starting dose of daprodustat in patients with moderate hepatic impairment is recommended to account for the increase in the systemic exposure of daprodustat.
L1614: We recommend reducing the starting dose of daprodustat by approximately half when initiating treatment in patients with moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B) except in patients
L1615: whose starting dose is already 1 mg, the lowest available strength of daprodustat. No adjustment of the starting dose is required in patients with mild hepatic impairment.
L1616: ## Severe Hepatic Impairment
L1617: The Applicant has not evaluated the effect of severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C) on daprodustat PK. Subjects with severe hepatic impairment and history of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis or fibrosis of the liver) were excluded from the phase 3 studies. The unbound exposure of daprodustat is expected to further increase in patients with severe hepatic impairment compared to moderate hepatic impairment due to more progressive hypoalbuminemia. As there is no PK and clinical safety experience for daprodustat in patients with severe hepatic impairment, use of daprodustat in patients with severe hepatic impairment is not recommended.
L1618: ## Other Intrinsic Factors
L1619: ## Renal Impairment
L1620: Daprodustat PK was evaluated in single dose (Study PHI112843) study in subjects with moderate to severe renal impairment and matched healthy cohort, and in a multiple dose study (Study PHI115573) in subjects with NDD renal impairment (Stages 3/4/5 CKD), and subjects with Stage 5 CKD on hemodialysis. Daprodustat PK following single or repeat doses was similar between subjects with moderate to severe renal impairment (CKD Stages 3 to 4) and their matched healthy controls (see Section 14.2 for details). Daprodustat PK was similar between subjects on hemodialysis on a non-dialysis day and subjects with moderate to severe renal impairment. Daprodustat is not significantly cleared by hemodialysis. For subjects with Stage 3/4 non-dialysis and Stage 5 CKD on hemodialysis (dialysis day), accumulation ratios for metabolites were up to 1.8-fold and 1.4-fold for the dialysis day and non-dialysis day, respectively, except for M13, for which accumulation ratio values were 2.6-fold and 1.5-fold, respectively.
L1621: The efficacy and safety of daprodustat in patients with CKD on dialysis or not on dialysis is primarily supported by the pivotal five global Phase 3 trials (ASCEND-ND, ASCEND-D, ASCEND-TD, ASCEND-ID and ASCEND NHQ) in these populations. No dose adjustment is needed for daprodustat in renal impairment.
L1622: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L1623: ## Drug Interactions
L1624: ## Metabolic Pathway
L1625: In vitro studies demonstrated that daprodustat is primarily metabolized by CYP2C8 (95% contribution), with a minor contribution of CYP3A4 (5% contribution), producing 6 predominant circulating metabolites, of which M2, M3, M13, are major metabolites. (\ge 10\%).
L1626: ## Effect of Other Drugs on Daprodustat
L1627: ## Effect of Strong CYP2C8 Inhibitors on Daprodustat
L1628: The drug-drug interaction (DDI) of daprodustat with gemfibrozil, a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor, was evaluated in a dedicated DDI study in healthy adults. Gemfibrozil 600 mg BID was dosed to steady state and its effects were evaluated on a single-dose of daprodustat 100 mg. Co-administration of a single-dose 100 mg daprodustat with gemfibrozil resulted in a 3.92-fold and 18.6-fold increase in daprodustat C_{max} and AUC_{(0-inf)}, respectively. This marked increase in both rate and extent of systemic exposure of daprodustat when co-administered with gemfibrozil is consistent with daprodustat being primarily metabolized by CYP2C8. The decrease in CYP2C8 metabolism of daprodustat is reflected by its ~4-fold increase in t_{1/2}, 2.51 to 9.26 h when co-administered with gemfibrozil. T_{max} was also delayed from 1.00 to 4.00 h.
L1629: Co-administration of daprodustat with strong CYP2C8 inhibitors (e.g., gemfibrozil) was contraindicated in the global Phase 3 studies. The review team agrees with the Applicant that the use of daprodustat should be contraindicated with strong CYP2C8 inhibitors in labeling.
L1630: ## Effect of Moderate CYP2C8 Inhibitors on Daprodustat
L1631: The Applicant did not conduct a dedicated in vivo DDI study of daprodustat with a moderate CYP2C8 inhibitor. However, the phase 2/3 trials including ASCEND-D allowed the use of clopidogrel, a moderate CYP2C8 inhibitor. The Applicant states that based on the Phase 2/3 PopPK analyses, co-administration of daprodustat with clopidogrel at steady state in 70 subjects showed that clopidogrel increases the exposure of daprodustat by 1.59-fold (90% CI: 1.39-1.82). PopPK analyses from previous Phase 2 and 3 clinical studies (GSK Reports 2019N405983_00 and 2019N405417_00) demonstrated up to 1.75- to 2.65-fold increase in daprodustat exposure when co-administered with clopidogrel (n=54 Phase 2 and n=22 Japan Phase 3 subjects).
L1632: However, the Applicant's current PopPK based DDI assessment is not adequate to accurately characterize the effect of concomitant medications on the PK of daprodustat in the pivotal Phase 3 clinical trials due to the following limitations: (a) A binary covariate analysis was performed in the Applicant's PopPK modeling; (b) An adequate number of daprodustat PK samples during the elimination phase were not available in the data from pivotal clinical trials; (c) There was a lack of data on medication history prior to study entry and dosing records for concomitant medications, such as, dose level, dose frequency, formulation, route of administration, start and stop date and clock time, duration, dose modification, etc. in the PopPK dataset.
L1633: Physiological based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) analyses showed that daprodustat AUC was increased by approximately 7.6-fold following coadministration with a single dose of 300-mg clopidogrel and approximately 4-fold following coadministration with maintenance doses of clopidogrel (75 mg). However, the effects of clopidogrel on daprodustat may be underestimated because the clopidogrel PBPK models used by the Applicant were not reliably validated and these clopidogrel models significantly underpredicted the clinically observed interactions between clopidogrel and repaglinide (see Section 14.6 for details). This suggests that the effect of clopidogrel on daprodustat exposure is expected to be no less than the model-predicted effects.
L1634: Although at least a 4-fold or higher increase in the AUC of daprodustat can be expected with concomitant administration of clopidogrel, no obvious trends were observed in the number of Hb increases per participant by baseline clopidogrel use, new clopidogrel use, or clopidogrel non-users in pooled data from studies 200807/ASCEND-D and 200808/ASCEND-ND.
L1635: **Figure 38** shows the mean evaluable hemoglobin and median assigned daprodustat dose by visit and by clopidogrel co-administration at baseline in patients from 200807/ASCEND-D. The mean Hb profile at each visit among clopidogrel users was similar to that in patients who are clopidogrel non-users. While these results support concomitant clopidogrel use with daprodustat, it is important to also compare daprodustat doses between clopidogrel users and non-users, since daprodustat is titrated based on Hb response. Interestingly, there was no consistent trend for a dose reduction of daprodustat in the clopidogrel users group compared to the non-users, as observed from the closely overlaying median and the corresponding distribution bars for daprodustat dose at each visit between the two groups, except for one step median dose decrease at the second visit (**Figure 38**).

L1641: Although, a decrease in the daprodustat dose is expected based on the predicted 4-fold or higher increase in exposure of daprodustat on concomitant clopidogrel administration, this was not reflected in the clinical experience with daprodustat in the pivotal Phase 3 trial. The reason for this observation is unclear, but the clinical experience from more than 100 patients who are clopidogrel users does support concomitant use of clopidogrel with daprodustat. That said, because of an expected 4-fold increase in daprodustat AUC on a background of clopidogrel at 75 mg, the review team recommends initiating clopidogrel users at a lower starting dose of
L1642: daprodustat to avoid exposure to high daprodustat concentrations during initiation except in patients whose starting dose is already 1 mg, the lowest available strength of daprodustat. For patients who may initiate clopidogrel while on daprodustat, the regular monitoring of Hb every 4 weeks should be adequate to inform the need for any dose adjustment of daprodustat.
L1643: ## Effect of CYP2C8 Inducers on Daprodustat
L1644: CYP2C8 is the primary CYP enzyme involved in the oxidative metabolism of daprodustat. Concomitant administration of drugs that are inducers of CYP2C8 may decrease daprodustat exposure. The Applicant proposed to monitor hemoglobin and adjust the dose of daprodustat as appropriate when initiating or stopping therapy with CYP2C8 inducer. The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposal.
L1645: ## Effect of BCRP Inhibitors on Daprodustat
L1646: In vitro data indicate daprodustat is a substrate of the breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) (efflux ratio ~4) and therefore has the potential for in vivo drug interactions due to BCRP-mediated inhibition (see Section 14.2 for details). BCRP inhibition-mediated drug interactions are known to primarily occur at the intestine, affecting absorption, and at the liver bile canaliculus membrane, affecting hepatobiliary secretion. Oral daprodustat is well-absorbed, with a calculated absorption fraction of 80%. Any intestinal BCRP inhibition would not be expected to lead to a 20% increase in absorption. Daprodustat has limited hepatobiliary clearance and is cleared primarily by oxidative metabolism. In the human ADME study following an IV infusion, daprodustat only represented 0.5% of total radioactivity in the duodenal bile, with oxidation metabolites accounting for the rest, and approximately 99.5% of the oral dose was excreted as oxidation metabolites, with daprodustat accounting for 0.5%. Based on the disposition profile of daprodustat, a clinically significant effect of BCRP inhibitors on daprodustat PK is not expected.
L1647: ## Effect of Acid Reducing Agents on Daprodustat
L1648: Daprodustat has a pH dependent solubility. Co-administration of daprodustat with acid reducing agents could increase solubility and thus potentially increase the systemic exposure of daprodustat. The Population PK model predicted up to 1.06-fold increase in C_{max} and 0.996-fold change in AUC of daprodustat with concomitant administration with acid reducing agents (N=526). Because oral daprodustat is well-absorbed, with a calculated fraction absorbed of 80%, any increase in absorption would not be expected to exceed 20%. A clinically significant effect of acid reducing agents on daprodustat PK is not expected.
L1649: ## Effect of Phosphate Binders and Oral Iron on Daprodustat
L1650: There is a potential for commonly co-administered medications such as oral iron and phosphate binders to affect the rate and extent of absorption of drugs including daprodustat. Co-administered oral iron (N=84) and phosphate binders (N=415), including sevelamer and aluminum, calcium, magnesium, and bicarbonate-based binders, were tested as potential covariates in the Phase 2/3 PopPK analysis. However, the Applicant's current PopPK based DDI assessment is not adequate to accurately characterize the effect of concomitant medications on the PK of daprodustat in the pivotal Phase 3 clinical trials due to the limitations of analysis
L1651: method and concomitant medication dosing history and records as detailed under a previous section discussing drug interaction with clopidogrel.
L1652: While a dedicated DDI study with oral iron or phosphate binders was not conducted, there is clinical experience from ASCEND-D for concomitant use of daprodustat with phosphate binders. Data from ASCEND-D shows that the phosphate binder user group in the daprodustat arm had a median dose of 6 mg compared to a one-step lower dose of 4 mg for the non-users. This likely reflects a potential interaction of daprodustat with phosphate binders per the expectation that a decrease in daprodustat exposure could lead to a higher maintenance dose to maintain Hb in the target range. That said, the extensive clinical experience from ASCEND-D supports the concomitant use of phosphate binders with daprodustat as it is shown that regular Hb monitoring and dose titration is adequate to manage a potential interaction. Although, a similar analysis has not been conducted for concomitant administration of oral iron, the recommended hemoglobin monitoring and the corresponding daprodustat dose titration algorithm seem adequate to support concomitant administration of oral iron with daprodustat.

L1663: ## 8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of Reproductive Potential
L1664: ## Animal Data
L1665: The following nonclinical data are used to support the label. Additional detailed information is available in Section 13 for nonclinical data.
L1666: **Table 112. Nonclinical Data Supporting Labeling on Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation**
L1667: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
8.1 Pregnancy	
Daprodustat was orally administered to pregnant rats at 0.5, 7, or 60 mg/kg/day from gestation day 6 to gestation day 17 during the period of organogenesis. No adverse effects were observed at doses less than or equal to 7 mg/kg/day (3 times the MRHD based on body surface area). Daprodustat administration resulted in post-implantation loss, increased embryofetal death, and reduction in skeletal ossification in rats at a dose of 60 mg/kg/day (24 times the MRHD based on body surface area), which was associated with maternal toxicity (reduced body weight gain or weight loss). Maternal toxicity occurred at doses associated with polycythemia.
Daprodustat was orally administered to pregnant rabbits at doses of 4, 30, or 60 mg/kg/day from gestation day 7 until gestation day 19 during the period of organogenesis. No adverse effects were observed at doses less than or equal to 30 mg/kg/day (24 times the MRHD based on body surface area).
Daprodustat administration was associated with low incidence of abortions and fetal skeletal malformations (irregularly shaped anterior fontanelle, manubrium, fused sternal centra, and microphthalmia) at a dose of 60 mg/kg/day (49 times the MRHD based on body surface area) in the presence of maternal toxicity (reduced body weight gain or weight loss) and polycythemia.
In a pre- and postnatal development study, pregnant rats were dosed orally with daprodustat from implantation until weaning (gestation day 6 to lactation day 21) at 0.8, 7, or 40 mg/kg/day concomitantly with 3 major human metabolites of daprodustat. No adverse effects were observed at doses less than or equal to 7 mg/kg/day (3 times the MRHD based on body surface area). Maternal toxicity was noted at 40 mg/kg/day, which represents 16-times the MRHD based on body surface area, which was associated with dystocia and increased pup deaths and decreased pup weights.
L1668: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
8.2 Lactation	In a pre- and postnatal development study in rats, when daprodustat was orally administered to maternal rats during the lactation period, the drug was detected in plasma of suckling pups on postnatal day 10. The plasma concentration of daprodustat in pups was 2.3% to 3.7% of daprodustat detected in the plasma of dams when dosed at 40 mg/kg/day.
13.1 Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility	Daprodustat was not carcinogenic in two-year carcinogenicity studies when administered orally at doses of 0.02, 0.1, 0.8, or 4 mg/kg/day (males)/ 7 mg/kg/day (females) in rats and 0.2, 0.8, or 3 mg/kg/day (including subcutaneous injection of major human metabolites of daprodustat) in mice. Daprodustat was negative for mutagenic or clastogenic potential in the in vitro bacterial reverse mutation assay, the in vitro human lymphocyte chromosomal aberration assay, and the in vivo rat bone marrow micronucleus assay. In a fertility and early embryonic development study in rats, daprodustat was administered orally at doses of 2, 7, or 100 mg/kg/day in females, resulting in maternal toxicity of reduced body weight gain and decreased mean uterine weight, associated with decreased number of corpora lutea, implantations, and live fetuses, and increased post-implantation loss at the dose of 100 mg/kg/day (41 times the MRHD based on body surface area).
L1669: Source: FDA Reviewer
L1670: Abbreviations: MRHD, maximum recommended human dose

L1672: ## Human Data
L1673: The Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health (DPMH) was consulted for advice on labeling text for Section 8.1 to 8.3 (Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling).
L1674: There are limited human pregnancy outcome data for daprodustat from the Sponsor's Pharmacovigilance Database. There were 9 pregnancies exposed to daprodustat identified in the clinical trials. The outcomes for these 9 pregnancies were
L1675: - 7 spontaneous abortions (SABs) at ages 6 to 19 weeks gestation (including both fetuses of one twin pregnancy)
- 2 elective abortions
- One normal live birth
L1676: There was no human pregnancy outcome data found in the published English language literature. The findings from animal studies suggest potential for fetal harm from exposure to daprodustat. Labeling will note that CKD is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, that animal data suggest harm, and that there are inadequate human pregnancy data.
L1677: Pregnancy would be expected to be uncommon in women in dialysis and a traditional pregnancy registry or a claims database study would likely be unsuccessful due to low enrollment. Therefore, DPMH recommends a PMR Descriptive Pregnancy Safety Study to follow-up on maternal and infant outcomes of pregnancies that do occur. Refer to Section 24 for a detailed summary of the PMR.
L1678: DPMH also recommends that the Applicant submit annual reports of daprodustat utilization rates amongst females of reproductive potential (females aged 15 to 50 years) calculated cumulatively
L1679: from the time of initial approval. If there appears to be substantial use of daprodustat in females of reproductive potential, then this would be considered new safety information that would trigger FDAAA and would result in the Agency issuing a PMR for a pregnancy registry study at that time.
L1680: There are no data on the presence of daprodustat in human milk, its effect on a breastfed infant or milk production. Parameters such as daprodustat's low molecular weight (~393 Daltons) and the presence of daprodustat in rat milk suggest it is likely that daprodustat will be present in human milk. The high protein binding (99%) suggest that the amount present is likely to be low. However, given the spectrum of serious adverse events that can be seen with daprodustat in adults, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with daprodustat and for one month after the last dose.
L1681: Given the low incidence of pregnancy and live births in the proposed population and recommendation against use during breastfeeding, a PMR for a lactation study would not be feasible and the alternative of performing a lactation study in healthy volunteers would not be ethically permissible in view of DPMH because a single dose of daprodustat could potentially cause thrombosis in a predisposed population of recently pregnant/locating women.
L1682: There were no clinical studies of the adverse effect of daprodustat on fertility. Recommendations for pregnancy testing or recommendations for contraception while taking daprodustat would not be appropriate given that the fetal harm warning is based on adverse effects in a single animal species at multiples greater than 10 times the maximum recommend human dose. Therefore, DPMH recommends that subsection 8.3 be omitted from the labeling.
L1683: For additional details regarding the DPMH review, refer to the consult review by Jane Liedkta M.D, Tamrar Johnson MD, MS and Lynne P. Yao, MD.

L1694: ## 11. Advisory Committee Summary
L1695: The Division of Non-Malignant Hematology (DNH) convened a virtual advisory committee meeting to discuss daprodustat on October 26, 2022. DNH sought the advisory committee's advice and recommendations on the safety issues discussed in this review and whether the benefits of daprodustat outweigh its risks in both the non-dialysis and dialysis populations.
L1696: The advisory committee members voted 5 yes vs. 11 no on the question of whether the benefits outweigh the risks for anemia of chronic kidney disease in patients not on dialysis. For the dialysis population, the vote was 13 yes vs. 3 no. Committee members recognized that the oral route of administration would provide convenience to some patients and another treatment option. However, the committee was concerned about the potential further increase in some cardiovascular risks seen only in the non-dialysis population when compared to the erythropoietin stimulating agent control, which itself carries these risks. See the Minutes and Transcript available on the external FDA website (fda.gov)20 for further details. Our actions on

L1701: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L1702: Daprodustat was granted approval for the treatment of adults with anemia due to chronic kidney disease (CKD) on or not on dialysis on June 29, 2020, in Japan.
L1703: Investigational New Drug Application IND 101291 was received on June 3, 2008, to study GSK1278863 (also referred to as daprodustat) for the treatment for anemia of chronic kidney disease. The initial IND included the protocol titled *PHX111427: A Phase I, Randomized, Single-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Dose-Escalation Study to Evaluate the Safety, Pharmacokinetics, and Pharmacodynamics of Single Oral Doses of GSK1278863A in Healthy Subjects*. The IND became active on July 3, 2008.
L1704: Transfer of IND 102191 ownership from GlaxoSmithKline to Octagon Research Solutions, Inc. was made on February 4, 2009. The ownership was transferred back to GlaxoSmithKline on March 1, 2011.
L1705: A Type C End of Phase 2A meeting was held on July 23, 2012, to discuss questions related to dosing. In addition, the Applicant proposed to conduct separate phase 3 trials to assess efficacy in two groups – patients requiring hemodialysis (HDD) and patients not requiring hemodialysis (non-dialysis dependent [NDD]), and planned to assess cardiovascular safety in a prospectively defined meta-analysis across their phase 3 trials. In terms of dosing, the Agency stated the Applicant's approach seemed reasonable and encouraged them to consider requesting another End of Phase 2A meeting with the Agency to discuss the details of their dosing modeling approaches to select the appropriate dose for their phase 3 trials. The Agency also commented that separate meta-analyses should be performed for NDD and HDD patients, instead of combining both populations, and recommended the Applicant to consider a superiority design for cardiovascular safety.
L1706: A carcinogenicity Special Protocol Assessment request was submitted for the proposed carcinogenicity protocol entitled *GSK1278863: A 2-year Oral (Gavage) Carcinogenicity Study in Rats* on August 16, 2013, and an agreement letter was issued on September 20, 2013. Another carcinogenicity Special Protocol Assessment request was submitted for the proposed carcinogenicity protocol entitled *GSK1278863: A 2 Year Carcinogenicity Study in Mice* on August 27, 2014, and an agreement letter was issued on October 8, 2014.
L1707: The Applicant submitted various meeting requests to obtain feedback and guidance in preparation for submission of a new marketing application for daprodustat. An End of Phase 2 meeting was held on February 22, 2016, to discuss the non-clinical and clinical program conducted to date and the phase 3 clinical development plan for daprodustat in the context of supporting a future NDA submission for daprodustat.
L1708: The Applicant's initial proposed proprietary name, [REDACTED](b) (4) was found unacceptable on August 14, 2019. Another proposed proprietary name review request was submitted with the proposed name of [REDACTED](b) (4), which was found to be conditionally acceptable on January 15, 2021.
L1709: Subsequently, the proposed proprietary name, (b)(4) was withdrawn by the Applicant on August 16, 2021.
L1710: A pre-NDA meeting took place on September 7, 2021, during which the Agency provided feedback on the Applicant's proposals for the content and format of the planned NDA submission and the Agency also provided comments on the high-level results for the daprodustat ASCEND phase 3 program.
L1711: The Applicant submitted another proposed proprietary name request with the proposed name of Jesduvroq, which was found to be conditionally acceptable on October 14, 2021.
L1712: The Applicant submitted the NDA on February 1, 2022, with the indication for the treatment of anemia due to chronic kidney disease in adult patients on dialysis and not on dialysis.

L1720: ## 13. Pharmacology Toxicology
L1721: ## 13.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application
L1722: ## 13.1.1. Primary pharmacology
L1723: Daprodustat is a reversible inhibitor of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-PH1, PH2, and PH3 which results in the stabilization and nuclear accumulation of HIF-1\alpha and HIF-2\alpha transcription factors, leading to increased transcription of the HIF-responsive genes, including erythropoietin. Treatment of daprodustat in vitro and in vivo pharmacology studies showed that daprodustat increases erythropoietin (EPO) levels (mRNA and protein), which results in an increase of red blood cell (RBC) parameters. Tabulated summary of the in vitro and in vivo pharmacology studies in animals conducted in support of daprodustat's mechanism of action are listed below. Daprodustat was coded as GSK1278863A in the pharmacology study reports.
L1724: **Table 114. Summary of the In Vitro and In Vivo Pharmacology Studies**
L1725: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Mechanism of action:
Biochemical Activity of the Prolyl Hydroxylase Inhibitor GSK1278863A/ UH2008/00036/01	
The effects of daprodustat on in vitro enzymatic activity of HIF PH3 and PH2, referred to as egg-laying deficiency protein nine-like protein 3 and 1 (EGLN3 and EGLN1) in the study report, were measured using a LANCETM (Homogeneous Time-Resolved Fluorescence Quenching Assay based on lanthanide chelates) format, a high-throughput homogeneous FRET assay. To evaluate the selectivity of daprodustat, two close homolog PHs, \alpha-ketoglutarate dependent iron dioxygenases CP4H and factor inhibiting HIF (FIH) were tested for inhibition.
Daprodustat competitively inhibited enzymatic activity of HIF-prolyl-hydroxylases PH3 and PH2 (K_i=1.8 and 7.3nM, respectively).
Daprodustat inhibited PHD3 with reversibility in a time dependent manner. The dissociation half-life (t_{1/2}) of daprodustat was 132 min, suggesting that daprodustat does not instantaneously dissociate and prolonged effect of daprodustat is possible.
Daprodustat did not strongly inhibit the CP4H and FIH with IC_{50} values in the \muM range >200\muM and 9.8\muM, respectively.

Activity of Prolyl Hydroxylase Inhibitor GSK1278863A and its Metabolites in Various Primary, Selectivity and Liability Assays/ 2011N121507/00	
The inhibition of enzymatic activity of other \alpha-ketoglutarate dependent iron dioxygenases and hERG and hNav1.2 channels (patch clamp assays) by daprodustat and its metabolites [M2; M3, M4, M5, M6 (both stereoisomers); M13] were tested to further investigate the pharmacological activity of metabolites of daprodustat. Daprodustat and its metabolites were also tested against eXP. eXP represents pharmacological targets from six target classes, comprising functional and binding assays. The constituent assays in eXP are mostly associated with clinical adverse events and/or drug side-effects. All data are derived from 11-point concentration-response curves. PH2, PH1, and PH3 were referred to as EGLN1, EGLN2, and EGLN3, respectively, in the study report.
L1726: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Daprodustat exhibited similar potency in inhibition of PHs in rats, dogs, and humans and selectivity against close homologs, collagen CP4H and factor FIH based on IC50 (nM) and Kiapp (nM) values.

L1734: The metabolites tested exhibited comparable pharmacological activity to the parent compound inhibiting PH1, PH2, and/or PH3 and comparable selectivity against CP4H and FIH with more than 800-fold selectivity for PHs vs. FIH; and, even higher for CP4H (IC50 &gt;100µM).

L1737: HIF Stabilization in Hep3B Cells after GSK1278863A Treatment/
UH2008/00026/00	
To investigate the stabilization of HIF1\alpha and HIF2\alpha as a result of inhibition of PHs, Hep3B cells, a hepatocellular carcinoma cell line, were incubated with 25 and 50 µM daprodustat or 100 µM deferoxamine (DFX, positive control) for 6 hours at 37°C. Nuclear protein was isolated, denatured, transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and incubated overnight with mouse monoclonal HIF1\alpha or rabbit polyclonal HIF2\alpha antibodies. Antibody-protein complexes were then detected using ECL-plus and visualized (qualitative assay only) using x-ray film.
HIF1\alpha and HIF2\alpha were detected with daprodustat or DFX treatment, while there was none detected in the vehicle group. The result shows that daprodustat induced HIF\alpha accumulation in the nucleus which indicates stabilization of both HIF1\alpha and HIF2\alpha.
L1738: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Drug activity related to proposed indication:
Erythropoietin and VEGF Protein Production in Hep3B Cells Treated with GSK1278863A/
UH2008/00024/00	
To investigate the effect of daprodustat on EPO and VEGF, Hep3B cells were incubated in duplicate with 0.026 to 100 µM (2.5-fold increase/concentration) daprodustat for 48 hours at 37°C. Media EPO and VEGF concentrations were then determined using an ELISA assay.
The average EPO EC50 was 3.3 µM and the average VEGF EC50 was 2.2 µM over 5 separate experiments. The average “maximum fold induction” relative to vehicle controls produced over the 5 experiments was 5.8 for EPO and 2.2 for VEGF. A bell-shaped concentration-response curve was observed with maximum EPO and VEGF levels consistently occurring at the 6.4 or 16 µM concentrations. Less than 75% viability was observed at 40 and 100 µM, suggesting toxicity at those concentrations.

Message Production in Hep3B Cells Treated with GSK1278863A/
UH2008/00027/00	
To investigate the downstream effects of PH inhibition by daprodustat, the changes in mRNA and/or protein levels of HIF-responsive genes, including EPO and VEGF-A were evaluated. Hep3B cells were incubated with 2.5, 12.5, and 25 µM daprodustat or 100 µM deferoxamine (DFX, positive control) for 16 hours at 37°C. TaqMan RT-PCR was then used to measure mRNA expression.
EPO mRNA expression was increased by 1.7-, 5.0-, and 7.4-fold, respectively, and HIF1\alpha-specific PGK1 mRNA expression was increased by 1.7-, 2.6-, and 2.9-fold, respectively, in daprodustat treated cells compared to vehicle control. DFX induced EPO and PGK1 mRNA expression 14- and 6.6-fold, respectively, compared to vehicle control. mRNA levels of PH2, PH1, and PH3 were not affected by daprodustat treatment, but were increased by 2.7-, 0.8, and 7.2 fold in DFX-treated cells. Daprodustat treatment also increased the level of EPO protein secreted from the cells and, to a lesser extent, secretion of VEGF protein.

Mouse Plasma Erythropoietin and VEGF Production after a Single Dose of GSK1278863A/
UH2008/00023/00	
To evaluate the effect of daprodustat on EPO and VEGF in PPP from normal female B6D2F1 mice, EPO and VEGF levels were determined using ELISA (n=6/timepoint) at 6 hours after treatment with vehicle and at 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, and 30 hours after administration of 60 mg/kg daprodustat via oral gavage. PPP was prepared by centrifugation of plasma samples for ELISA analysis.
Daprodustat treatment increased plasma EPO levels by 11-fold (vs. control) which peaked at 12 hours after daprodustat treatment. A 1.2- to 1.8-fold increase in VEGF compared to vehicle control was observed at all timepoints.

L1742: Mouse Erythropoietin Message in Liver and Kidney after a Single Dose of GSK1278863A/
UH2008/00022/00	
Normal female B6D2F1 mice were dosed with 60 mg/kg daprodustat, and blood samples were collected (n=5/timepoint) at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, and 16 hours after administration of daprodustat (vehicle controls collected at the 4, 8, and 12 hour timepoints) via oral gavage. To evaluate the effect of daprodustat on EPO protein level in plasma, PPP samples were prepared and analyzed by ELISA. Additionally, liver and kidneys were collected at the 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 hours after administration timepoints to evaluate EPO and PGK1 mRNA expression using TaqMan RT-PCR (normalized to GAPDH).
Daprodustat treatment at 60 mg/kg in mouse induced EPO liver mRNA expression and plasma protein levels exhibited a biphasic response with peaks at 8 and 12 hours after dosing. EPO liver mRNA expression increased from 279-fold (relative to vehicle control) observed at 2 hours after dosing to 449-fold at the 6-hour time point. Liver EPO mRNA expression then decreased to 31-fold at the 8-hour time point, then was increased again at the 12-hour timepoint (279-fold; 10-hour timepoint was not evaluated). Kidney EPO mRNA expression was increased by 56-fold and 35-fold, respectively, at the 8-hour and 12-hour timepoints. PGK1 expression was minimally affected by daprodustat-treatment.

Mouse Hemoglobin Increases after 8 Doses of GSK1278863A/
UH2008/00028/00	
Female B6D2F1 mice (n=5/group) were treated with single daily oral doses of 0 (vehicle), 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg daprodustat for 8 consecutive days to evaluate the effects of daprodustat on erythropoiesis. Animals were euthanized 24 hours after the last dose and blood was collected for hematology parameter analyses.
Daprodustat treatment increased RBC parameters including RBC count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and reticulocytes (up to 17%, 17%, 25% and 673%, respectively vs. control) and decreased platelet/white cell counts with dose-relation compared to the vehicle control.
L1743: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Rat Hemoglobin Increases after GSK1278863A Treatment In Vivo/
UH2008/00025/00	Male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=5/group) were treated with oral doses of daprodustat at 0 (vehicle), 0.3, 1, 3, or 10 mg/kg for 21 consecutive days to evaluate the effect of daprodustat on erythropoiesis. Blood was collected on Day 8, 15, and 22 for hematology parameter analyses.
Daprodustat treatment resulted in dose-related increases in RBC parameters (up to 18%, 22%, and 26% of RBC, hemoglobin, and hematocrit, respectively) that were evident by Day 8 and further increased on Day 22. There were no significant drug-related effects on white cell counts.

L1746: ## 13.1.2. Secondary Pharmacology
L1747: To characterize any potential activity associated with daprodustat beyond its understood mechanism of action, secondary pharmacology studies were conducted screening for the activity in vitro of daprodustat on a range of binding uptake sites expressed on tissues/organs.
L1748: **Table 116. Summary of Secondary Pharmacology Studies**
L1749: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Study of GSK1278863A in Various Receptor Binding and Enzyme Assays (CEREP Screen)/
UH2008/ 00031/00	To assess the selectivity of daprodustat in 50 receptor binding, ion channel and transporter assays unrelated to direct PH inhibitory activity, CEREP profiling (in vitro assessment of the effect of drug on 50 targeted receptors/ion channels/enzymes) was performed at the selected concentration of 10 µM daprodustat in order to screen for off-target potential.
There was no significant (<20%) inhibition observed in any of the 50 assays, indicating that daprodustat has low potential to cause unintended effects through any of the receptors and enzymes in the panel.
L1750: Study/ Study No.	Findings
Effect of GSK1278863A on the Activity of Rat Cyclooxygenase/ CH2008/ 00030/00 & Selectivity against protein kinases/ UH2008/00036/00	
To investigate any potential inhibitory activity of daprodustat for the protein kinase enzymes, daprodustat was evaluated against cyclooxygenase 1 and 2 enzymes (COX1 and COX2) and 7 protein kinases [CDK-2/Cyclin A, PLK1, 70 kDa ribosomal protein S6 kinase I (p70S6K), SRC1, DYRK3 (also known as YAK3), VEGFR-2 and rat RSK1].
Daprodustat weakly and reversibly inhibited COX1 activity with an IC50 value of 66 µM, which suggests low likelihood of functional inhibition in vivo. Daprodustat had no effect on COX2 activity. It is unlikely that the COX1 inhibition by daprodustat is directly contributing to the adverse effects on stomach, considering the unbound concentration of daprodustat needed to inhibit COX1 by 50% is 764-fold higher than the maximum free drug concentration (Cmax) at the maximum recommended human dose.
The IC50 values for all protein kinases tested were >10µM which suggests that daprodustat selectively inhibits PHs (with lower IC50 values in nM range) vs. the protein kinases.
L1751: Source: Reviewer's analysis

L1753: ## 13.1.3. Safety Pharmacology
L1754: - Daprodustat had no effect on hERG channel activity (up to 47.66µM), neurobehavioral, and respiratory activity (up to 20 mg/kg).
- Mild cardiovascular effects of daprodustat including small magnitude of QT and QRS prolongation was observed in ex vivo study with rabbit left ventricular wedge at concentrations ≥10µM.
- Mild reversible increase in heart rate was observed in rats after repeated oral dosing of daprodustat for 5 days at doses of ≥30 mg/kg and did not alter the mean arterial pressure.
L1755: ## 13.1.4. ADME/PK

L1803: ## Blood to Plasma Ratio
L1804: - The blood to plasma and blood to liver ratios were tested in Sprague Dawley rats with a single oral dose of 10 mg/kg [^{14}C]-radiolabeled daprodustat (CD2008/00100). The highest mean concentrations of radioactivity of blood, plasma, and liver (37.4-76.1 and 22.2-30.7 µg equiv/g, respectively) were observed at 1 hour post dose in males and females. Low association of radioactivity with blood cells were noted with blood to plasma ratio 0.505-0.560 and mean liver to blood ratios (0.319-0.825) decreased through 24 hours post dose.
- The blood to plasma ratio was 0.84 µg equiv/g in dogs (intact) (CD2008/00025) and the average blood to plasma concentration ratios were 0.64 µg equiv/g for both intact and BDC monkeys.
L1805: ## Whole Body Distribution
L1806: - In the Long Evans rat, the tissue radioactivity was evaluated with [^{14}C]-radiolabeled daprodustat (CD2008/00271/00) and the result exhibited that daprodustat was widely distributed into the tissues tested (CNS [Brain, choroid plexus, meninges, peripheral nerve, and spinal cord], glands [adrenal, pineal, pituitary, thyroid, lachrymal, harderian, pancreas, salivary], fat [brown or abdominal], skin [non-pigmented or pigmented], reproductive organs [prostate gland, epididymis, and testis], skeletal muscle [skeletal and heart], respiratory tract [lung and nasal turbinates], GI tract mucosa [esophagus, cecum, small/large intestine, and stomach], and ocular tissue [lens and uveal tract]).The highest radioactivity concentrations at any timepoint were observed in the GI tract. For most non-GI tract tissues, the highest radioactivity concentrations were observed at 1 h, including in the blood, aorta, lung, and meninges.
- The radioactivity concentrations were low in the brain suggesting little penetration of the blood brain barrier.
- The only radioactivity detected by Day 7 was low levels observed in peripheral nerves and large intestine contents.
- Radioactivity concentrations in the uveal tract, pigmented skin, and meninges peak at 1h or 4h declining steadily afterwards until undetectable by Day 7. This finding suggests no irreversible binding to melanin-containing tissues.
L1807: ## Metabolism
L1808: - Intrinsic clearance of daprodustat was low in the liver microsomes and hepatocytes of mouse, rat, dog, monkey, and human based on clearance (CLi) data (UH2008/0018).
- Total of 19 metabolites of daprodustat were identified, of which 14 metabolites were detected in human hepatocytes.

L1811: ## Excretion
L1812: Single oral administrations of [^{14}\text{C}] daprodustat to intact male and female rats and dogs and to male monkeys, and to BDC male rats, dogs, and monkeys (CD2008/00100, CD2008/00025, and 2018N355713) showed that feces is the major route of elimination of daprodustat in intact animals. Urinary and biliary recoveries indicated that they are minor routes of elimination and the highest blood radioactivity concentrations were observed at 1 hour after dosing, and the majority of recovered radioactivity was excreted within the first 24 hours.

L1818: ## 13.1.5. Toxicology
L1819: ## 13.1.5.1. General Toxicology
L1820: General toxicology studies of 4- and 13-weeks duration were conducted in Sprague Dawley rats and Beagle Dogs with rats receiving daily oral doses by gavage and dogs by capsule. A 13-week toxicity study was also conducted in the cynomolgus monkey with daily dosing by oral gavage. Toxicities in rats were overall consistent with toxicities observed in the 26-week rat study and were mainly due to exaggerated pharmacology (see Section 13.2). Higher doses were tolerated in the 4- and 13-week rat studies compared to the 26-week rat study. The 100 mg/kg/day dose administered to rats in the 13-week study toxicity resulted in severe toxicities to the heart (valvulopathy, atrial thrombus, valvular thrombus, endocardial hyperplasia, and cardiomyopathy), lung (chronic passive congestion), kidney (infarct, thrombus, cortical tubular pigment and tubular basophilia), brain (focal degeneration) and stomach (glandular erosion/ulceration, submucosal inflammatory cell infiltrate, hemorrhage, and vascular medial hypertrophy). Multifocal erosions, ulcers, hemorrhage, edema, and/or inflammation in the glandular region of the stomach were observed at doses as low as 7 mg/kg/day in the 4-week study. Toxicities in dogs were due to the exaggerated pharmacology of daprodustat related to polycythemia and hyperviscosity of the blood leading to poor tissue perfusion and anoxia. In monkeys, there were fewer organs of toxicity (only bone marrow [erythroid hypercellularity], lung [alveolar hemorrhage], thymus [lymphoid atrophy], and stomach [hemorrhage and effects
L1821: on body weight and clinical signs/chemistry)] in the 13-week study compared to the 39-week study, but the toxicities in the 13-week study were more severe at the higher dose tested of 100 mg/kg/day (see Section 13.2).

GLP compliance: Yes
Study is valid: Yes	
Sprague Dawley male rats (n=3/group) were administered 2 oral doses of 1000 or 2000 mg/kg, approximately 24-hours apart.
The mean % proportion of immature polychromatic erythrocytes (PCE) was reduced by ~23% at ≥1000 mg/kg/day daprodustat. In addition, a statistically significant 2-fold increase in micronucleated PCE (MPCE) frequency that exceeded the upper 98% tolerance limit of historical controls was observed in the 2000 mg/kg/day daprodustat group. There was also a slight increase (approximately 1.6-fold) in group mean reticulocyte count observed in treatment groups compared to the control group. The result was positive, but it is not considered to be a direct genotoxic response based on the small magnitude of the response and the mechanism of action of GSK1278863A which can contribute to the positive result.

GSK1278863A: Effects
on Hepcidin Expression
in Hep3B Cells/
UH2009/00011/00	
Reduced hepcidin level is known to increase the utilization of the iron to produce hemoglobin and HIF and hypoxia have been shown to suppress hepatic hepcidin expression in mice. To investigate the effects of daprodustat on the iron regulation protein hepcidin, Hep3B cells were treated with BMP-6 to induce levels of hepcidin for 6 hours. Cells were then treated with daprodustat at 1.56-25 µM or recombinant human EPO at 0-100 mIU/mL for 48 hours. TaqMan RT-PCR was used to measure hepcidin mRNA expression.
L1835: ## **Drug activity related to proposed indication:**
L1836: Effect of GSK1278863A and its metabolites on EPO Expression in Hep3B Cells/
2012N134715/00	
To evaluate the effects of daprodustat and its metabolites on induction of EPO protein, Hep3B cells were incubated with 3 and 30µM daprodustat and its predominant metabolites (M2; M4; M3, M4, M5, M6 (both stereoisomers); M13) for 24 hours. Human EPO levels were measured using the Meso Scale Discovery Assay. The experiment was conducted twice with confluent and sub-confluent cell density.
Daprodustat elevated EPO levels in a dose dependent manner, but EPO induction was not shown by the metabolites tested at 3 or 30 µM.

GSK1278863A:
Erythropoietin Response
Following a Single Oral
Dose in Sprague Dawley
Rats/ 2011N126015/00	
Male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=3-5/group) were treated with doses of daprodustat at 0 (vehicle), 1, 3, 10 or 30 mg/kg as a single dose or once daily for 3 consecutive days via oral gavage. Plasma EPO and VEGF levels and EPO, VEGF, PDK1, and GLUT-1 mRNA in the liver were measured.
EPO and VEGF levels in plasma were not increased with single or 3 daily oral doses of daprodustat. Although, the EPO mRNA expression in liver was dose-dependently increased at ≥10 mg/kg 6 hours post-dose (up to 324X vs. control). HO-1 mRNA expression (up to 18X vs. control), was also increased at 30 mg/kg, 6 hours post-dose.

L1839: ## 13.2.3. General Toxicology
L1840: **Title/ Study No.: GSK1278863A: A 26-week Oral (Gavage) Toxicity Study in the Rat/ 2011N126130**
L1841: ## Key Study Findings
L1842: - Daprodustat (GSK1278663A) produced drug-related mortality at 10 mg/kg/day. Seven main study and four toxicokinetic (TK) males were found dead or euthanized. Due to mortality and toxicity observed at 10 mg/kg/day, all surviving males in this group were pre-terminally euthanized during Week 20 (Day 135/134). Cause of death appeared related to hemorrhage, systemic thrombosis and/or necrosis and thrombosis of various organs including the heart, lung, kidney, and cecum. These findings are consistent with the drug's primary pharmacology and secondary impact on hemodynamics.
- Moderately higher reticulocyte (~70% ↑) and red blood cell counts (29-41% ↑) were observed by week 26/27 in males and females at 10 mg/kg/day. Females could tolerate the elevations (reticulocytes up to 82% ↑, red blood cell counts 39% ↑), but males could not.
- Systemic thrombosis, hemorrhage, and necrosis were observed at 10 mg/kg/day and in the heart and lung of males at 10 mg/kg/day.
- The no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) was determined at 4 mg/kg/day based on the mortality and drug-related toxic effects observed at 10 mg/kg/day.

Serum cardiac troponin	At doses of 0.8 and 4 mg/kg/day, increased serum troponin (cTnI) values in individual treated males at Week 13 were between 3.7- and 5.8-fold, relative to the highest concurrent control value of 0.051 µg/L. Potassium (K) concentrations were decreased in males and females at 10 mg/kg/day during Week 4 (down to 0.81X) and at ≥ 4 mg/kg/day (down to 0.86X) during Week 13, which seems to be a daprodustat effect on HIF.

enlarged adrenal glands (2/12, corresponds to cortical hypertrophy), and pale/depressed area of kidney (5/12, corresponds to necrosis/infarction) were observed in HD males. L1886: ## **Title/ Study No.:** GSK1278863A: A 39-week Oral (Gavage) Toxicity Study in the Cynomolgus Monkey with a 6-week Recovery Period /2011N126131
L1887: ## **Key Study Findings**
L1888: - One mortality (unscheduled termination due to moribundity) occurred at LD but the cause of death is not determined.
- Lower body weight gain was noted in all daprodustat-treated groups, but the findings resolved after the recovery period.
- Daprodustat-related increase of RBC mass, reticulocytes, and serum iron parameters at \ge10 mg/kg/day was observed, related to the direct pharmacological effect of daprodustat, and corresponding evidence of erythropoiesis were noted including congestion in multiple organs (kidneys, liver, brain, and eye) or whole body, skin reddening, and bone marrow erythroid hypercellularity.
- Other drug-related microscopic findings include gastric hemorrhage, erosions and/or ulcerations in the stomach, pigment deposits in kidney, mononuclear cell infiltration of choroid plexus, and degeneration of skeletal muscle, and these findings persisted after the recovery period.
- One high dose (HD) female presented partly closed right eye (ptosis of the right upper eyelid) and anisocoria (mydriasis of the right pupil) and congestion of the retinal vessels at \gemid dose and optic disc hyperemia at HD were observed at the end of dosing period which persisted with decreased incidence/severity at the end of recovery period.
- The NOAEL is determined at 3 mg/kg/day based on the microscopic findings in choroid plexus, kidney, and stomach at \ge10 mg/kg/day.

L1893: **Table 139. Observations and Results of the 39-Week Oral (Gavage) Toxicity Study in the Cynomolgus Monkey With a 6-Week Recovery Period /2011N126131**
L1894: Parameter	Major Findings
Mortality	One LD male was terminated due to moribundity on Day 262 (Week 38). Diarrhea and liquid feces, significant body weight loss and changes in clinical chemistry (decreased neutrophil count, decreased urea, albumin, total protein, total calcium, phosphorus and cholesterol concentrations, increased potassium concentrations) were consistent with protein loss and poor clinical condition. The cause of death could not be determined at the time of necropsy. This animal had bone marrow hypocellularity, thickening of the wall of the small intestine with moderate muscular hypertrophy/hyperplasia in the jejunum, mild multifocal acinar cell atrophy in the pancreas, marked thymus lymphoid atrophy, and minimal fibrosis of the lung and spleen. TK analysis shows that this animal was not exposed to higher levels of test article compared to other animals in the group. Metabolite levels were not measured in this animal. This mortality appears unrelated to the test article (lack of dose response and comparable findings to animals at higher doses).
Clinical signs	Daprodustat related findings were noted:Skin reddening, primarily on the cranium, with dose dependence was observed in all monkeys with higher incidence. Other affected locations include but are not limited to: gums and/or mouth, fore limbs, hind limbs, abdominal area and ventral thoracic and/or cervical region. Scabby skin was more frequently observed in higher number of HD males.
Dose-related changes in feces (soft and/or liquid, color change to green/pale) was noted and liquid vagina discharge was observed in females treated with daprodustat.
Red skin at the right periorbital area and right eyelid, partly closed eyes (right eye, ptosis and mydriasis) was observed in one HD female (No. 453) between dosing Days 138-149. Eye position, movements and pupillary light reflexes were normal. These observations led to the hypothesis of an oculomotor nerve palsy supported by the histological brain findings (localized inflammation [superficial brainstem/nerve root] and concurrent changes including edema and hemorrhage). Findings were fully or partially reversible.
L1895: Parameter	Major Findings
Body weights	Daprodustat-related lower body weight gain was observed in daprodustat-treated groups. The drug-effect on the body weight gain resolved after the 6-week recovery period. After this recovery period, the body weight of HD males was comparable to the controls and HD females recovered from minor differences in body weight gain by the end of dosing

L1922: **Organ weights** Daprodustat-related changes in organ weights (% relative to body weight) were noted. Increased organ weights of heart up to 21% and 19%, kidney up to 17% and 15%, liver up to 20-24% were noted at HD in males and females, respectively. L1923: **Histopathology** Daprodustat-related findings were noted in multiple tissues/organs including brain, bone marrow, kidneys, stomach, and the whole body. Increased hypercellularity of bone marrow and iron deposition in kidney are associated with direct pharmacological effect of daprodustat. Findings in the brain (mononuclear cell infiltration in the choroid plexus and subacute inflammation, edema, and hemorrhage in the superficial brainstem) and stomach (hemorrhage and ulceration of glandular mucosa) are considered daprodustat-related adverse findings which showed trend of recovery but persisted after the recovery period.

Toxicokinetics	The systemic exposure of daprodustat based on the C_{max} and AUC increased with dose increment with less than dose-proportional manner. The sex difference was less than 2-fold between male and female and the t_{max} ranged from 0.5 to 8 hours. The metabolites of daprodustat [GSK2391220 (M2), GSK2531403 (M3), GSK2499166 (M4), GSK2531399 (M5), GSK2531398 (M6) and GSK2531400 (M13)] were detected in plasma in all drug-treated groups with increased exposure with dose increment and the metabolite to parent ratios exposures (AUC) were less than 0.09. The maximum plasma concentrations for the metabolites were generally observed between 1 and 8 hours after dosing during Week 39.

L1939: ## 13.2.4. Reproductive Toxicology
L1940: ## 13.2.4.1. Fertility and Early Embryonic Development
L1941: **Title/ Study Number:** GSK1278863A: Oral (Gavage) Once Daily Male Fertility Study in the CrI:CD(SD) Rat/ CD2009/00389/00
L1942: ## Key Study Findings
L1943: - Daprodustat-related death occurred in 20 mg/kg/day HD males (2/25).
- Daprodustat-related noteworthy findings were mostly at HD, which include dark red discoloration of kidney, liver, and stomach.
L1944: - Daprodustat had no effect on reproductive potential in male Sprague Dawley rats up to 20 mg/kg/day.
L1945: GLP Compliance: Yes
L1946: **Title/ Study Number:** GSK1278863A: Oral Female Fertility and Early Embryonic Development Study in Rats/ CD2009/00236/00
L1947: ## Key Study Findings
L1948: - Maternal toxicity at HD of 100 mg/kg/day includes significant decrease in body weight gain (BWG) during the premating period of Day 0-14 (80%) and up to gestation Day 7 (28%) with corresponding food consumption decrease up to 15% compared to controls.
- In HD females, statistically significant decrease of mean uterine weight (19%), number of corpora lutea (14%), number of implantations (15%), number of live fetuses (21%), and a marked increase of total postimplantation loss were observed.
- There were no effects on estrous cycles, days needed for mating, and mating and fertility indices up to 100 mg/kg/day.
- NOAEL for maternal toxicity, female fertility, and embryo-fetal development in rats is 7 mg/kg/day based on the GSK1278863A-related adverse findings in HD.

L1959: **Title/ Study Number:** GSK1278863A: Oral (Gavage) Once Daily Embryo Fetal Development Study in the Crl:CD(SD) Rat/ CD2009/00388/01 (aka Study No. AFA00832)
L1960: ## Key Study Findings
L1961: - Maternal toxicity at the HD of 60 mg/kg/day (significant decreases in body weight gain (BWG; -21% overall) and food consumption (FC) compared to controls during the dosing period).
- There was a 7% decrease in gravid uterine weights, 6.5-fold increase in post-implantation loss, 15% decrease in mean litter size, and 4.4-fold increase in the percentage of fetuses dead or resorbed in litters with one or more live fetuses in HD females compared to controls.
- Skeletal variations of slight-delayed ossification were observed, which often are related to maternal toxicity.
- NOAEL for both maternal toxicity and embryo-fetal development is defined at 7 mg/kg/day based on decreased BWG and uterine weight of dams, and increased post-implantation loss and fetuses death/resorption associated with maternal toxicity.

L1974: **Necropsy findings**
All daprodustat-treated groups displayed increases in the litter and fetal percentages of skeletal variations when compared to historical and concurrent controls. These findings are not considered adverse as they represent developmental delays due to maternal toxicity and would reverse.

Other noteworthy findings not included in the labeling based on low incidence (1 fetus in 1 litter/dose level) were:

- One fetus with a cleft in the palate and snout in the HD group. A cervical rib was present at the 7th cervical vertebrae in two fetuses, one each in the 7 and 60 mg/kg/day groups.
- One fetus had a misaligned arch in a sacral vertebra and misaligned ileum in the HD group.

L2034: ## 13.2.4.3. Prenatal and Postnatal Development (PPND)
L2035: **Title/ Study Number:** GSK1278863A + metabolites [GSK2391220A (M2), GSK2506104A (M3) and GSK2531401A (M13)]: Oral Gavage and Subcutaneous Injection Tolerability, Toxicokinetics and Pre- and Postnatal Developmental Dose Range Study in Pregnant Rats/ 2016N305715/00
L2036: Pregnant Sprague Dawley rats were treated with daprodustat at 0 (1% methylcellulose) or 60 mg/kg/day with (Group 2, 3) or without (Group 1) metabolite cocktail (M2, M3, and M13) SC injection twice daily (6 hours between doses). A metabolite cocktail was prepared at 2 different sets of doses, 1X or 3X: 2.5, 3.2, or 1.8 mg/kg/day or 7.5, 9.6, or 5.4 mg/kg/day of M2, M3, or M13, for Group 2 and 3, respectively. Main study animals were dosed from GD 6 to LD 6 and TK study animals were dosed from GD 6 to GD 10. The extended duration study (Group 4-7) with a decreased dosing regimen of 0, 10 or 40 mg/kg/day daprodustat was conducted with or without the metabolite cocktail (2.5, 3.2, or 1.8 mg/kg/day, M2, M3, and M13, respectively).
