L2659: ## 15. Study/Trial Design
L2660: ## 15.1. Study 200808/ASCEND-ND
L2661: ## Protocol Amendments
L2662: There were 4 global amendments and 5 “country specific” local amendments to the original protocol (dated June 2016). Protocol Amendment 05 (dated July 20, 2020) was used to prepare the clinical study report (CSR) submitted with the application.
L2663: ## Amendment 01
L2664: Amendment 01 was implemented September 20, 2016 and applied to: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. The main changes to the protocol included clarification of the end of the study definition/criteria. The study rationale and inclusion criteria were revised. Additional guidance was added to the iron management criteria, and a new exploratory objective to compare the effect of daprodustat to rhEPO on delayed graft function (DGF) after deceased donor kidney transplantation was added.
L2665: ## Amendment 02
L2666: Amendment 02 was implemented October 12, 2016 and applied to all countries and sites. It also included country-specific requirements for France and Czech Republic. The main changes to the protocol included the changes from country-specific Amendment 1. The section relating to darbepoetin alfa pre-filled syringe incidents, malfunctions and user errors was deleted. The Schedules of Assessments were modified to include new timepoints and prompts. The negatively adjudicated events reporting process was updated. Historical kidney ultrasound and a provision for a more sensitive imaging study (e.g., MRI, CT) to assess entry criteria were added.
L2667: ## Amendment 03
L2668: Amendment 03 was implemented October 5, 2017 and applied to all countries and sites. The main changes to the protocol included a provision for possible adjustment to the Dose Adjustment Algorithm triggers for Hb values 7.5 g/dL to &lt;9.5 g/dL based on the review of blinded instream aggregate Hb data. Retest values for Hb and transferrin saturation (TSAT) to determine eligibility at Week -8 were added. Exclusion criteria were broadened. A provision was added for unexpected circumstances where the supply to the site was interrupted. New darbepoetin alfa dose strengths (not available in all countries) were added. Directions regarding randomized treatment and study continuation for participants away from the research site for an extended period of time were added.
L2669: Clarifications were made to the timeframe for iron management criteria. Visit windows were revised and clarified. The FSH level to confirm menopause was updated.
L2670: The Schedules of Assessments were modified for clarification and to include new activities and prompts. The additional inclusion and eligible visits to collect PK samples in PK sub-studies were clarified. The patient reported outcome (PRO) section was updated to add healthcare resource utilization data.
L2671: The statistical section was revised to change from two-sided testing at the 5% level to one-sided testing at the 2.5% level; to clarify progression of CKD endpoint population and analysis model and for secondary endpoints; to change significance levels to p-values; to correct the timepoint for various PROs; to add a more complete description of the adjustments to statistical model; and to add additional text regarding the interim analysis process. Exploratory endpoints around Hb variability, iron parameters, transfusions, and dose adjustment scheme were added.
L2672: Adjustments to the objectives, endpoints and analysis of the ABPM sub-study were made.
L2673: ## Amendment 04
L2674: Amendment 04 was implemented August 16, 2019 and applied to all countries and sites. The protocol was modified to add retest values for Hb at Day 1, an additional opportunity for TSAT to determine eligibility at Week -8, and revised the definition of current uncontrolled hypertension in order to determine eligibility. Hypothetical risk information, new required assessments, and randomized treatment stopping criteria for participants with ADPKD were added.
L2675: Worsening of hypertension was added as an adverse event of special interest.
L2676: Renal progression via change in eGFR was added as a secondary objective/endpoint.
L2677: For participants transitioning to dialysis, clarified the last historical clearance (Kt/V_{urea}) measurement obtained per standard of care can be used. Stated recruitment in the ABPM sub-study was closed in Amendment 4. Entry criteria to PK sub-study was revised; if the sub-study recruitment did not make its pre-specified target, depending on the number of participants with data, a limited number of analyses and data summaries may be produced.
L2678: ## Amendment 05
L2679: Amendment 05 was implemented July 30, 2020 and applied to all countries and sites. The protocol was modified to revise the major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) non-inferiority margin; as a result, the target MACE was also revised (to 664 events). The primary rationale for these changes was to accelerate the closeout of the study in consideration of the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on study integrity and data quality. Additionally, this change was aligned with similar studies that had already compared the effects of HIF-PHIs on MACE versus rhEPO, based on publicly available information. Analysis of the Hb co-primary endpoint and the multiplicity adjustment strategy were updated. Pregnancy reporting timelines were updated to align with revised Sponsor timings.
L2680: It should be noted that because the adjudication process for MACE may have taken time, some MACE related analyses contain more than 664 events.
L2681: ## Protocol Deviations
L2682: Significant protocol deviations were reported for 66% of subjects in the daprodustat arm and 68% of subjects in the darbepoetin alfa arm. The majority of protocol deviations were due to study procedures/assessments (44%) of total population (N=3872) and were balanced between arms.
L2683: In Study 200808 (ASCEND-ND), data on 17 study participants were excluded from all analyses as a valid informed consent was never obtained. During the conduct of the study, three sites (223710, 228130, and 239601) were closed early due to good clinical practice (GCP) non-compliance issues including suspected fraud at one site. The site (23601) with suspected fraud randomized one subject and the data from this site were included in the study displays. No additional analyses were performed to exclude the participant's data from this site. Data from site 228130 were included in the study displays except for one screen-failed participant who did not have a valid informed consent form. Data from site 223710 were not included in the data displays due to invalid consent obtained from 14 participants at this site.
L2684: Additional quality issues relating to GCP noncompliance (e.g., informed consent, dosing errors, late reporting of serious adverse events (SAEs), unreported temperature excursions, central lab issues, late reporting of individual case safety reports, missing research records) were identified at other sites and corrective actions taken, and issues were reviewed for root causes and addressed by Applicant.
L2685: ## 15.2. Study 200807/ASCEND-D
L2686: ## Protocol Amendments
L2687: There were 3 global amendments and 4 “country-specific” local amendments to the original protocol (dated June 9, 2016). Protocol Amendment 04 (dated July 30, 2020) was used to prepare the CSR. A copy of Protocol Amendment 04 and each of the protocol amendments is found in the modular appendix. A brief summary of each protocol amendment is provided below.
L2688: ## Amendment 01
L2689: Amendment 01 was implemented September 20, 2016 and applied to: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. The main changes to the protocol included clarification of the end of the study definition/criteria. The study rationale and inclusion criteria were revised. Additional guidance was added to the iron management criteria, and a new exploratory objective to compare the effect of daprodustat to rhEPO on delayed graft function (DGF) after deceased donor kidney transplantation was added.
L2690: ## Amendment 02
L2691: Amendment 02 was implemented October 12, 2016 and applied to all countries and sites. It also included country-specific requirements for France and Czech Republic. The main changes to the protocol included the changes from country-specific Amendment 1. The section relating to darbepoetin alfa pre-filled syringe incidents, malfunctions and user errors was deleted. The Schedules of Assessments were modified to include new timepoints and prompts. Text was added to clarify participants randomized to rhEPO who transition from hemodialysis to peritoneal dialysis change from epoetin alfa to darbepoetin alfa. Text relating to the timing of dialysis in relation to the study visit was amended. The negatively adjudicated events reporting process was updated. Historical kidney ultrasound and a provision for a more sensitive imaging study (e.g., MRI, CT) to assess entry criteria were added.
L2692: ## Amendment 03
L2693: Amendment 03 was implemented October 5, 2017 and applied to all countries and sites. The main changes to the protocol included a provision for possible adjustment to the Dose Adjustment Algorithm triggers for Hb values 7.5 g/dL to &lt;9.5 g/dL based on the review of blinded instream aggregate Hb data. Retest values for Hb and TSAT to determine eligibility at Week -8 were added. Exclusion criteria were broadened. Guidance for those receiving hemodialysis two times a week randomized to the epoetin alfa arm and to require three times a week epoetin alfa dosing was added. A provision was added for unexpected circumstances where the supply to the site was interrupted. New darbepoetin alfa dose strengths (not available in all countries) were added. Directions regarding randomized treatment and study continuation for participants away from the research site for an extended period of time were added.
L2694: Clarifications were made to the timeframe for iron management criteria, the “frequency of dialysis” inclusion criterion, the valid study visit days by dialysis type, and the Baseline dose for the purposes of the rescue algorithm for participants switching from hemodialysis to peritoneal
L2695: dialysis who are randomized to rhEPO. Visit windows were revised and clarified. The FSH level to confirm menopause was updated.
L2696: The Schedules of Assessments were modified for clarification and to include new activities and prompts. The additional inclusion and eligible visits to collect PK samples in PK sub-studies were clarified. The PRO section was updated to add healthcare resource utilization data.
L2697: The statistical section was revised to change from two-sided testing at the 5% level to one-sided testing at the 2.5% level; to correct the comparator for the Null and Alternative hypotheses; to change significance levels to p-values; to add a more complete description of the adjustments to statistical model; to update hyporesponder analyses; and to add additional text regarding the interim analysis process. Exploratory endpoints around Hb variability, iron parameters, transfusions, and dose adjustment scheme were added. Adjustments to the objectives, endpoints and analysis of the ABPM sub-study were made.
L2698: ## Amendment 04
L2699: Amendment 04 was implemented July 30, 2020 and applied to all countries and sites.
L2700: The protocol was modified to add retest values for Hb and TSAT in order to determine eligibility. The MACE non-inferiority margin was revised; as a result, the target MACE was also revised (to 664 events). The primary rationale for these changes was to accelerate the closeout of the study in consideration of the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on study integrity and data quality. Additionally, this change was aligned with similar studies that had already compared the effects of HIF-PHIs on MACE versus rhEPO, based on publicly available information. Analysis of the Hb co-primary endpoint and the multiplicity adjustment strategy were updated.
L2701: Please note that the protocol amendment was approved after 664 events had already occurred during the study. This means that some MACE related analyses contain more than 664 events.
L2702: ## Reviewer's Comments
L2703: The amendments did not negatively impact the study design, conduct or results of the study.
L2704: ## Protocol Deviations
L2705: Significant protocol deviations were reported for 7% of the participants in the daprodustat arm and 81% of participants in the rhEPO arm. The majority of protocol deviations were due to study procedures/assessments (44%) of the total population (N=2964) and were balanced between arms. The protocol deviations recorded likely did not have an impact on the interpretation of the results.
L2706: Eight sites were closed due to ongoing GCP non-compliance and three of the 8 closed sites were closed due to research conduct, which included suspected fraud. The data from these 3 sites were included in the primary study displays and to assess the impact of the sites on the overall study conclusion, a supportive analysis was conducted, excluding the data from these 3 sites. The results from supportive analyses, conducted by the Applicant, did not show a significant impact on the primary endpoints when all randomized participants were excluded from these sites.

L2788: ## 16.2. ASCEND-NHQ Statistical Analysis Plan
L2789: ## Sample Size Determination
L2790: Approximately 600 participants were planned to be randomized (300 per arm) to receive daprodustat or placebo, who would be treated to achieve and maintain Hb between 11 and 12 g/dL.
L2791: Under the assumption that up to 10% of participants would withdraw from the study before Week 24 (start of EP), 600 randomized participants would result in at least 540 evaluable participants.
L2792: For the primary endpoint, the expected difference in mean Hb change from baseline and the EP, between arms, was 1.0 g/dL and the anticipated between participant standard deviation was 1.5 g/dL, based on historical rhEPO trials and daprodustat clinical trial experience to date. The planned study size would provide more than 99% power for superiority on Hb. In addition, it was anticipated that the smallest difference in mean Hb change between arms that would meet the statistical criterion for superiority would be 0.25 g/dL.
L2793: For the first key secondary endpoint of % of participants having a Hb increase of \ge1.0 g/dL from baseline to EP, 540 evaluable participants would provide &gt;90% power to detect a 20% difference between daprodustat and placebo, assuming 30% of placebo arm participants would have a Hb increase of \ge1.0 g/dL. In that case, the smallest difference between daprodustat and placebo that would meet the statistical criterion for superiority would be 8%.
L2794: ## Missing Data Handling for Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L2795: Multiple imputation analysis was performed using all available Hb values (on and off-treatment) and conducted under a set of assumptions about missing Hb values.
L2796: - For each of the missing dataset (out of the 200 imputed as indicated above), the missing scheduled Hb values through Week 28 were imputed based on different scenarios. The ANCOVA regression had region, treatment, baseline Hb, off treatment status, and prior scheduled (possibly imputed) Hb values as covariates. Missing data were handled as either being on-treatment or off treatment, with the former being imputed with only on-treatment data and the latter being imputed with only off-treatment dataMissing data were classified as being on-treatment, ifPatients died, used non-randomized ESA Medication, received blood transfusions while on treatment
- Study Drug Interruption (e.g., temporarily stopped treatment due to COVID, then restarted)
- Missing data were classified as being off-treatment, ifTreatment discontinuation
- Patients died, used non-randomized ESA Medication, received blood transfusions after treatment discontinuation
- The low and high cutoff Hb values of 6 g/dL and 15 g/dL were applied to all imputed Hb values.
- EP Hb values were computed and compared across treatment groups using the primary ANCOVA model described above. Rubin's rules were used to combine results of the imputed datasets using SAS PROC MIANALYZE procedure. As a result, a single estimated treatment difference and its standard error was produced, with which a 95% CI was calculated.
L2797: ## Analysis for Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L2798: The primary efficacy estimand was the effect of daprodustat treatment relative to placebo regardless of adherence to treatment, the use of non-randomized ESA medication for any reason including rescue therapy, or the use of blood transfusions, in participants defined by the inclusion/exclusion criteria and assuming participants did not die before the end of the EP.
L2799: The primary efficacy endpoint was the mean change in Hb between baseline and over the EP (mean of all available [on and off treatment] Hb values for Week 24 through Week 28, inclusive, including any unscheduled Hb values that were taken during this time period). To quantify the difference in mean Hb change, an ANCOVA model adjusted for treatment, baseline Hb, and region was used. The primary model provided a two-sided 95% CI and one-sided superiority p-value for the difference in the primary Hb endpoint between the daprodustat and placebo arm. Superiority would be established if the one-sided p-value was less than 0.025.
L2800: ## Sensitivity Analysis
L2801: A sensitivity analysis that considers an “on-drug” efficacy estimand was conducted. In this analysis, only Hb values measured while the participant was taking randomized study medication was included. Missing Hb values were imputed based on the reasons for the missing Hb data.
L2802: ## Analyses for Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
L2803: For the endpoint of % of participants having a Hb increase of \ge 1.0 g/dL from baseline to EP, the EP Hb value was defined as the mean of all available Hb values (on- and off-treatment) during
L2804: the EP (Week 24 to Week 28, inclusive). A CMH chi-squared test that adjusted for treatment and region was used to make comparisons between the treatment groups. A treatment policy strategy was used as in the primary analysis to include all on- and off-treatment Hb values of the ITT populations, including values taken after discontinuation of study treatment/rescue therapy. Missing data were imputed as described for the primary efficacy analysis.
L2805: For the key secondary endpoint of mean change in SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain score between baseline and Week 28, a hypothetical strategy, including only on treatment values, was used assuming participants had not had intercurrent events of death prior to the end of the EP and randomized treatment discontinuation prior to the end of the EP. Data collected after discontinuation of study treatment/rescue medication were not included in the analysis and were treated as missing. The SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain scores after discontinuation of study treatment were imputed based on the conservative assumption that there was no change in the domain scores after the intercurrent event, so the last available on-treatment values (or baseline values if there was no on-treatment value) were used in the imputation. Missing SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain scores were imputed based on a missing at random assumption. An ANCOVA model was used including factors for baseline score, treatment, and region. The analysis was performed for both 0-100 scoring and norm-based scoring. The 0-100 scoring was considered as the primary results and norm-based as supportive results.
L2806: ## Additional Secondary Endpoints
L2807: For the Hb responder analysis, mean Hb during the EP was defined as the on-drug supportive analysis. Responders were participants with a mean Hb during the EP that fell within the Hb analysis range of 11 to 12 g/dL. A CMH chi-squared test that adjusted for treatment and region was used to compare the number and % of responders between the treatment groups. The one-sided CMH p-value was compared to 0.025 to assess nominal significance.
L2808: For the time to stopping study treatment due to meeting rescue criteria, a Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for the baseline categorical values of treatment and region was used. Confidence intervals (CIs) for the rate per 100 person-years was also reported. For within-group rates, the two-sided 95% CI was obtained using an exact Poisson method. For difference in rates between treatments, the two-sided 95% CI was constructed with a normal approximation using Wald's method. One-sided p-values were compared to 0.025 to assess nominal significance.
L2809: Secondary endpoints included the mean change from baseline in Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S) score and each Chronic Kidney Disease Anemia Questionnaire (CKD-AQ) domain score and single items were analyzed using a mixed model repeated measures approach with an unstructured covariance matrix to compare the difference in means between arms. The models were fitted to data collected after Baseline up to Week 28, using on-treatment values and excluded the measures taken after discontinuation of study treatment. The models included factors for treatment, time, region, treatment by time interaction, corresponding baseline score values (i.e., PGI-S score, CKD-AQ domain, and CKD-AQ single items score in the corresponding model), and the baseline score by time interaction. Analyses were done with the MIXED procedure in SAS, using the Kenward-Roger option to estimate denominator degrees of freedom and standard errors. A point estimate and two-sided 95% CI for the adjusted mean treatment difference (daprodustat - placebo) and a one-sided superiority p-value for this test at
L2810: Week 28 were provided. One-sided p-values were compared to 0.025 to assess nominal significance.
L2811: For the % of participants having an improvement in SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain score \ge 6 from baseline at Week 28, a CMH chi-squared test that adjusted for treatment and region was used to make comparisons between the treatment groups. This was based on the 0-100 scoring. As with the second key secondary endpoint, on-treatment SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain scores were used and excluded the measures taken after discontinuation of study treatment.
L2812: The mean change from baseline in SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain scores (individual items of the Vitality domain, overall score of the Physical Function domain), EuroQol 5 Dimension 5 Level (EQ-5D-5L) score, and EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale (EQ-VAS) score were analyzed using a mixed model repeated measures approach with an unstructured covariance matrix to compare the difference in means between arms. The models were fitted to HRQoL data collected after Baseline up to Week 28, using on treatment values and excluded the measures taken after discontinuation of study treatment. The model included factors for treatment, time, region, treatment by time interaction, corresponding baseline value (HRQoL parameter or utility scores), and the baseline value by time interaction term.
L2813: ## Multiple Comparison
L2814: The primary endpoint based on mean change from baseline on Hb value was tested first for superiority using a one-sided 2.5% significance level. Conditional on achieving statistical significance, the two key secondary endpoints would be tested for superiority using a one-sided 2.5% significance level sequentially. The additional secondary/exploratory endpoints were not adjusted for multiplicity. Summary statistics and nominal one-sided 2.5% significance levels were used to describe the results of these treatment comparisons.
L2815: ## Subgroup Analysis
L2816: Subgroup analysis including age, sex, and race was performed using all available Hb values (on- and off- treatment, including imputed values) and separately using evaluable Hb values only. The ANCOVA models used in the primary analysis was used and adjusted for treatment, baseline Hb, region, subgroup, and subgroup treatment interaction term.
L2817: For the first key secondary endpoint (% of participants having a Hb increase of \ge 1.0 g/dL from baseline to EP), subgroup analysis was performed using all available Hb values (on- and off- treatment). A CMH chi-squared test that adjusted for treatment and subgroup was used to make comparisons between the treatment groups.
L2818: For the second key secondary endpoint, subgroup analyses were performed using an ANCOVA model that included factors for baseline score, treatment, region, subgroup, and subgroup treatment interaction.
L2819: ## 16.2.1. Review of the 36-item Short Form Health Survey version 2.0 (SF-36 v2.0) Vitality Domain for Evaluation of Clinical Benefit
L2820: The Applicant used the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain to assess the secondary efficacy PRO endpoint in ASCEND-NHQ. This instrument was reviewed for content validity, other measurement properties, and meaningful within-patient change.
L2821: ## 16.2.1.1. Instrument Description
L2822: The SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain (Figure 64 in Section 16.3.1) is a 4-item domain within the SF-36 v2.0, which is designed to assess some aspects of fatigue related to fullness of life, energy, feeling tired, and feeling worn out. Each item is rated on a 5-point verbal rating scale ranging from “None of the time” to “All of the time.” The recall period is the previous 7 days (“past week”).
L2823: Each item score of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain ranges between 1 to 5. The four items in the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain are first summed to calculate a raw domain score that ranges from 4 to 20. Of note, the positively worded items (feeling “full of life” and having energy) are reverse scored (i.e., a response value of 1 corresponds to a raw score value of 5). The raw domain score is then converted to a 0-100 scaled score by the formula shown below, where higher scores indicate better health, and lower scores indicate more disability (or worse health state):
L2824: 0\text{-}100 \text{ scaled SF-36 Vitality score} = \left(\left(\text{SF-36 Vitality domain raw sum score}\right) - 4\right)/16 \times 100
L2825: To limit missing data at the item-level, the SF-36 v2.0 was administered in an electronic format and respondents were not permitted to skip items.
L2826: ## 16.2.1.2. Content Validity
L2827: The Applicant completed the following instrument development activities to evaluate the content validity of the SF-36 Vitality domain in patients with anemia associated with CKD:
L2828: - A literature review
- Patient input (published qualitative study, reanalysis of existing patient interview transcripts)
L2829: The review team evaluated the data generated from these instrument development activities. Both literature and patient input (from published qualitative study and reanalysis of patient interview transcripts) confirmed that the content of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain was relevant to the patient experience with anemia due to CKD. While the SF-36 v2.0 has been widely used across different diseases, the Applicant did not cognitively test the SF-36 v2.0 with patients with anemia due to CKD to evaluate patient comprehension. However, the Applicant cited a published qualitative study that conducted cognitive interviews in patients with type 2 diabetes and anemia due to CKD; this literature provides limited details regarding patient comprehension of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain.
L2830: Refer to the full COA review by the DCOA for detailed results of the content validity of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain.
L2831: ## 16.2.1.3. Other Measurement Properties (Reliability, Construct Validity, Responsiveness)
L2832: The Applicant evaluated the other measurement properties of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain using combined data from two phase 3 trials in adult patients with anemia associated with CKD:
L2833: - ASCEND-ND (n=350): A randomized, open-label, active controlled, parallel-group, multi-center, event-driven study in non-dialysis subjects with anemia associated with CKD.
- ASCEND-ID (n=100): A randomized, open-label, active-controlled, parallel-group, multi-center study in subjects with anemia associated with CKD who were not routine ESA users and were initiating dialysis.
L2834: The Applicant's rationale for combining the data from the two trials was to ensure a full representation in the sample among a broad range of patients with CKD across the continuum of the disease—from non-dialysis to those who were previously not on dialysis, but subsequently required the initiation of dialysis. It's unclear why data from ASCEND-D were not included as well.
L2835: Two 'refresh samples21' were used to evaluate the measurement properties of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain. Both refresh samples 1 and 2 comprised 350 ASCEND-ND participants. A further 100 ASCEND-ID participants were also included in refresh sample 1. Of the 100 ASCEND-ID participants included in refresh sample 1, 50 were randomly selected to also be included in refresh sample 2. For more details regarding the refresh samples, refer to Section 2.2 in Appendix 20 of the Applicant's SF-36 PRO Dossier ("EVA-28889-01: Confirmation of the Psychometric Properties of the SF-36 Vitality Scale Among Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease" report Version 1.0 dated July 26, 2021).
L2836: Based on FDA's assessment, the quantitative sample used for psychometric analyses is not fully comparable to the study population of ASCEND-NHQ. Despite this, the reliability (internal consistency and test-retest reliability) and convergent validity of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain appear to be within acceptable and reasonable ranges. The results for assessment of known groups validity (a form of construct validity) were difficult to interpret as the Applicant's selected known groups (i.e., Hb, CKD stage, dialysis status, PGI-S, CKD-AQ Items 1 and 2) did not adequately categorize patients by the severity of fatigue-related symptoms. The Applicant did not evaluate the responsiveness of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain using the refresh samples. Instead, the Applicant cited publications to support the responsiveness of this instrument. The review team acknowledges that the responsiveness of this instrument has been widely published, however, it remains difficult to fully evaluate the responsiveness of this instrument solely on literature given the considerable variability observed in the context of use (e.g., design of studies).
L2837: 21 The samples are termed 'refresh' as they were also used to confirm psychometric properties of the CKD-AQ.
L2838: Refer to the full COA review by the DCOA for detailed discussion of the other measurement properties of the SF-36 v2.0 Vitality domain.

L2914: ## 17. Clinical Safety
L2915: ## 17.1. Missing Data Sensitivity Analyses
L2916: The Applicant conducted pre-specified tipping point sensitivity analyses under a range of missing data assumptions, in addition to non-informative censoring, to determine the assumptions that would change the non-inferiority conclusions for MACE. Assumptions about missing outcomes in the daprodustat and control arms varied independently and included scenarios where subjects with missing data on daprodustat had worse outcomes than subjects with missing data on control. Patients who prematurely withdrew22 from the study without a known first MACE prior to study withdrawal were multiply imputed in bootstrap samples under
L2917: 22 Withdrawal includes withdrawal of consent, lost to follow-up, and study site closure
L2918: a range of event rate scenarios. As requested by the FDA during the NDA review, the follow-up period for all subjects was from randomization to the date of study completion/withdrawal, excluding deaths after this time.
L2919: For each treatment arm, the assumed event rates ranged from all prematurely censored subjects had a MACE at the time of censoring to all prematurely censored subjects completed the study without experiencing the event. These event rates, including a censored-at-random scenario, were quantified using the log-hazard rate ratio comparing prematurely censored subjects to observed subjects (Jackson et al. 2014). For each pair (daprodustat, control) of log-hazard rate ratio, the imputed time to first occurrence of MACE in a bootstrap sample was then compared between treatment groups using the primary analysis Cox proportional hazards model.23 Rubin's rules combined the result (hazard ratio) of the Cox proportional hazards model for 200 imputed datasets. HR estimates were reported with the assumed hazard rate ratio and number of events for the missing subjects in each treatment arm. Interpretation of sensitivity analysis results required an assessment of the plausibility of the assumptions regarding: (1) missing subjects' event rate relative to observed subjects' event rate in each treatment arm; and (2) missing subjects' event rate in the daprodustat arm relative to the control arm.
L2920: Using the same imputation method, the Applicant also explored the impact of missing secondary safety endpoint information for the adjudicated endpoints: all-cause mortality, CV mortality, MI, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, and thromboembolic event. Unlike MACE, for which missing data assumptions that changed (tipped) the non-inferiority conclusion could be identified, secondary safety endpoints were tested but not controlled for multiple comparisons; therefore, the determination of which missing data assumptions were plausible and would result in a concerning hazard ratio required an abundance of judgement, because there was not a multiplicity controlled test as a point of reference. In that regard, the interpretation of sensitivity analyses for secondary safety endpoints were limited and not presented. Only MACE tipping point analyses results are shown.
L2921: ## ASCEND-ND
L2922: In the primary analysis of MACE, 61/1937 (3%) daprodustat and 61/1935 (3%) darbepoetin alfa subjects were censored. The time to event analysis results of MACE, with deaths excluded after study completion/withdrawal, was HR 1.05 (CI 0.93, 1.21)24 with incidence rates of: daprodustat 367/1937 (19%); darbepoetin alfa 356/1935 (18%). Note that the HR estimate is slightly different from the pre-specified primary analysis result of MACE that included deaths after study completion/withdrawal (see discussion in Section 7.4). Sensitivity analyses (Figure 68) to the non-informative censoring assumption in the MACE primary analysis showed that the results (HR 1.09; 95% CI 0.4, 1.26) tipped, i.e., did not rule out the 1.25 risk margin, when daprodustat-treated, censored subjects were assumed to have 19/61 (31%) MACE and a (worse) hazard rate of 1.7 times the daprodustat-treated, observed subjects, and darbepoetin alfa-treated, censored
L2923: 23 Primary analysis of time to first MACE was a Cox proportional hazards model controlling for treatment and adjusting for the following baseline variables used in stratified randomization: region (Asia Pacific, Eastern Europe/South Africa, Western Europe/Canada/ANZ, Latin America, USA), current ESA use (ASCEND-ND only: User, Non-user), and dialysis type (ASCEND-D only: HD, peritoneal dialysis).
L2924: 24 Sponsor response (dated June 10, 2022) to information request
L2925: subjects were assumed to have 4/61 (7%) MACE and a (better) hazard rate of 0.4 times the darbepoetin alfa-treated, observed subjects. A less extreme assumption (daprodustat 1.7, darbepoetin alfa 0.6) resulted in HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.93, 1.25), which did not tip the MACE results away from non-inferiority (Figure 69, estimate 1.08 boxed in green). Note that assuming a hazard rate ratio of 1.0 in each arm is equivalent to the non-informative censoring assumption.
L2926: Comment: The MACE rate assumptions in the daprodustat and darbepoetin alfa arms (1.7 vs 0.4 times the event rate of observed subjects) that censored darbepoetin alfa-treated subjects have a lower MACE rate than the observed darbepoetin alfa-treated subjects could be considered implausible for a tipping point in an active-controlled study. A limitation of these analyses was that the Applicant did not consider patients that failed to have a CV endpoint assessment during or after the EOS window to be missing outcome data. Although including these subjects could increase the number of subjects missing to be approximately 5%25 in each treatment arm, missing data were low and similar across arms. The primary analysis result for MACE, assuming non-informative censoring, was tipped only under fairly extreme assumptions of daprodustat having more MACE while the active control having less MACE than the observed subjects. Therefore, the primary analysis assuming non-informative censoring could be relied upon for interpretation.

L2948: ## 17.3. CV Events in Relation to Average Dose Summaries Exploratory Analyses
L2949: We explored the relationship between dose level and each adjudicated CV endpoint in studies ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND. The endpoints included MACE, all-cause mortality, CV mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, and thromboembolic events. For subjects who experience more than one adverse event with the same preferred term or more than one adverse event within a grouping of preferred terms, the first adverse event was used for analysis, and exposure time used in the calculation of total patient-years was censored at the date of the first adverse event. We focused on the dosing frequency adjusted on-treatment CV period, which is the endpoint ascertainment window defined as the period starting from the
L2950: treatment start date to the earlier of the date of study completion/withdrawal or last non-zero dose date + dosing frequency28 + 28 days (OT + Dosing Frequency + 28).
L2951: Dose was analyzed by:
L2952: - Average dose while receiving treatment
- Average dose received during the 4 weeks preceding the event
- Average dose received during the 2 weeks preceding the event
- Average dose at the time of the event
L2953: In “average dose while receiving treatment” analysis, overall average weekly study drug dose was calculated for each subject until the first occurrence of the event for subjects with the event or until the end of the ascertainment window for subjects without the event. Each of these overall averages were assigned to one of five fixed dose categories.29 The number of events were tabulated by for each dose category in each treatment group and expressed as a percent of subjects with events.
L2954: Because these drugs were titrated to effect throughout the treatment period, alternative analyses were conducted using a moving average of the dose. In “average dose received during the 4 weeks preceding the event” analysis, average weekly dose during the 4 weeks prior to the event of interest was calculated for every subject until the first occurrence of the event of interest for subjects with the event or until the end of the ascertainment window for subjects without the event. For example, the dose at Week 16 was the average dose during Weeks 13 through 16. The average weekly dose was assigned to one of five fixed dose categories. A similar analysis was conducted using two-week intervals preceding the event, which was referred to as “average dose received during the 2 weeks preceding the event.” In “average dose at the time of the event” analysis, the weekly dose at the time of the event was defined as the dose on the day the event occurred, converted to a weekly dose, and assigned to a dose category. In these three analyses, the count of subjects with an event, total person-years (PY), rate per PY and rate per 100 PY were calculated for each dose category and each treatment group.
L2955: Summary tables and figures were created for each endpoint by treatment arm (daprodustat, control) for each study (ASCEND-ND, ASCEND-D). Results are not shown.
L2956: Summary: Higher percentages or incidence rates observed at higher dose categories for some CV endpoints including MACE in both treatment arms. Limitations with the interpretability of these analyses included: (1) potential bias in treatment (daprodustat vs. control) effect comparison using an on-treatment analysis that has the potential to break the integrity of randomization and introduce bias as there may differences between treatment arms in the types of subjects that adhere to treatment; (2) potential confounding by disease severity in the relationship between CV
L2957: 28 1 day (daprodustat); 7, 14, or 28 days (darbepoetin alfa); 2 or 7 days (epoetin alfa).
L2958: 29 Sponsor determined the dose categories based on the possible doses in each treatment arm of each study. Dose categories differed by arm and can differ by the dose categorization (while receiving treatment, 4 weeks preceding the event, 2 weeks preceding the event, at the time of event). Categories were chosen to “balance the representation of a range of doses across the categories, while having sufficient amount of observation time in each dose category to permit meaningful examination of the data.”
L2959: event by dose level; and (3) data sparsity for most events except for MACE and all-cause mortality.
L2960: ## 17.4. CV Events in Relation to Average Hemoglobin Summaries
L2961: We explored the relationship between hemoglobin (Hb) level and each adjudicated CV endpoint in studies ASCEND-D and ASCEND-ND. The endpoints included MACE, all-cause mortality, CV mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, and thromboembolic events. For subjects who experience more than one adverse event with the same preferred term or more than one adverse event within a grouping of preferred terms, the first adverse event was used for analysis, and exposure time used in the calculation of total patient-years was censored at the dated of the first adverse event. We focused on the dosing frequency adjusted on-treatment CV period, which is the endpoint ascertainment window defined as the period starting from the treatment start date to the earlier of the date of study completion/withdrawal or last non-zero dose date + dosing frequency30 + 28 days (OT + Dosing Frequency + 28).
L2962: Hb was analyzed by:
L2963: - Hb just prior to the event
- Hb rate of change over the 4 weeks preceding the eventSeparate analysis for rates of increases and decreases
- Hb rate of change over the 12 weeks preceding the eventSeparate analysis for rates of increases and decreases
L2964: For each treatment arm, Hb just prior to the event of interest was defined as the last on-treatment Hb just prior to the event. This was calculated for every subject until the first occurrence of the event for subjects with the event or until end of treatment of subjects without the event. The number of events were tabulated for each Hb quintile, determined from all Hb values, indicating how many subjects had an event in that quintile for their given Hb associated with the event. Total PY, rate per PY, and rate per 100 PY were calculated for each quintile.
L2965: Another Hb analysis explored the Hb rate of change (g/dL/week) over the 4 weeks preceding the event. Using the subject's treatment start date as the anchor date, a 4-week interval was created up to either the event of interest or the end of the ascertainment window if they did not have an event. Then a Hb slope was calculated by fitting a linear regression line through the Hb values obtained during the 4 weeks. For example, the slope at Week 8 was calculated from Hb values obtained on Weeks 5, 6, 7, 8. The slopes were categorized as either positive (including zero) or negative slopes. Quintiles were created based on the positive slopes and separately, for the negative slopes. The number of events, total PY, rate per PY, and rate per 100 PY were calculated for each Hb quintile. The analyses were repeated for rate of change over the 12 weeks
L2966: 30 1 day (daprodustat); 7, 14, or 28 days (darbepoetin alfa); 2 or 7 days (epoetin alfa).
L2967: preceding the event. Of note, Hb slopes could be only estimated for a limited number of events, because Hb assessments were scheduled less frequently later in the trials (at least every 4 weeks during the first year of the trial and at least every 12 weeks thereafter), and two values were necessary to calculate a slope.
L2968: Summary tables and figures were created for each endpoint by treatment arm (daprodustat, control) for each study (ASCEND-ND, ASCEND-D). Results are not shown.
L2969: Summary: Higher incidence rates observed at lower Hb quintiles for some CV endpoints including MACE in both treatment arms. Limitations with the interpretability of these analyses included: (1) potential bias in treatment (daprodustat vs. control) effect comparison using an on-treatment analysis that has the potential to break the integrity of randomization and introduce bias as there may be differences between treatment arms in the types of subjects that adhere to treatment; (2) potential confounding by disease severity in the relationship between CV event by Hb level; and (3) data sparsity for most events except for MACE and all-cause mortality.
L2970: ## 17.5. Subgroup Analyses by ESA Use – ASCEND-ND
L2971: To further explore CV endpoints among baseline ESA users versus non-users in the NDD population, exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted for each adjudicated CV endpoint. For all these CV endpoints, a higher incidence was observed with daprodustat compared to darbepoetin alfa among ESA users and non-users at randomization, except CV MACE and MI among ESA non-users (Figure 72). The variability (CI widths) of HR estimates depended on the number of events and sample sizes, with lower precision for endpoints like stroke and thromboembolic events. In summary, analyses of ESA use subgroups did not indicate a consistently higher risk among ESA users compared to non-users, but the elevated HR estimates in both subgroups across multiple CV endpoints corroborated the unfavorable results in the overall study population.

L3021: ## 24. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L3022: ## Draft Daprodustat PMRs for Dialysis Dependent Population
L3023: Final language will be in the action letter.
L3024: **PMR 1:** Conduct a prospective observational study to characterize the long-term safety (up to 5 years follow up) of JESDUVROQ in adults with dialysis dependent chronic kidney disease treated with the approved dosing regimen of JESDUVROQ (b) (4). Specific safety outcomes of interest include: the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) defined as all-cause mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke; thrombotic vascular events to include vascular access thrombosis; hospitalization for heart failure; serious gastrointestinal bleeds and eye disorders (proliferative retinopathy). The study population should include adults previously treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and adults naïve to ESAs. The effect of baseline and maximum achieved hemoglobin on the specified safety outcomes should be evaluated. Submit an integrated safety dataset and patient level data including JESDUVROQ dosing, treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs), adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation, and outcomes of SAEs with your final report.
L3025: Draft Protocol Submission:	08/2023
Final Protocol Submission:	02/2024
Interim Report Submission:	07/2028
Study Completion:	07/2031
Final Report Submission:	07/2032
L3026: **PMR 2:** Conduct an observational study (up to 5 years follow up) to assess the risk for malignancy (hematological and non-hematological) in dialysis dependent chronic kidney disease adults with anemia treated with JESDUVROQ versus an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) comparator arm. The study should include an assessment of primary malignancies among adults with no cancer history (including assessment by type and location), and the impact of JESDUVROQ on progression-free survival, and overall survival in adults with prior cancers.
L3027: Draft Protocol Submission:	12/2024
Final Protocol Submission:	06/2025
Study Completion:	10/2031
Final Report Submission:	10/2032
L3028: **PMR 3:** Conduct a worldwide descriptive study to collect prospective and retrospective data on women exposed to JESDUVROQ during pregnancy to assess the risk of pregnancy and maternal complications, adverse effects on the developing fetus and neonate, and adverse effects on the infant. Assess infant outcomes through at least the first year of life. The minimum number of patients will be specified in the protocol.
L3029: Draft Protocol Submission:	08/2023
Final Protocol Submission:	02/2024
Interim Report Submission:	09/2027
Study Completion:	08/2029
Final Report Submission:	09/2030
L3030: **PREA PMR:** Conduct a trial to evaluate the pharmacokinetics and safety of daprodustat for the treatment of anemia associated with chronic kidney disease in children and adolescents aged 3 months to under 18 years requiring dialysis. (b) (4)
L3031: Study Completion:	08/2029
Final Report Submission:	02/2030
L3032: (b) (4)
L3033: We request that you submit all adverse events received or otherwise obtained from foreign or domestic sources of possible thrombotic vascular events (TVE), heart failure (HF), gastrointestinal erosion (GE), and hypertensive crisis as 15-day “Alert reports” (described under 21 CFR 314.80(c)(1)). Include a summary and analysis of these adverse events (i.e., TVE, HHF, GE and hypertensive crisis) that are serious in the narrative portion of your periodic adverse drug experience report (PADER) required under 21 CFR 314.80(c)(2), quarterly during the first 3 years post-approval and annually thereafter, through the 5 year following the initial U.S. approval date.
L3034: The summary analyses should include an assessment of all new information obtained during the reporting interval and cumulatively since initial U.S. approval related to these adverse events (i.e., TVE, HHF, GE and hypertensive crisis) with the aim of further characterizing these risks (e.g., indication, temporal association, action taken, outcome, de-challenge/re-challenge, confounders, underlying risk factors, use in unapproved populations such as non-dialysis-dependent patients, and assessment of causality).
L3035: We also request that, in the narrative portion of your annual PADERs, you submit annual reports of daprodustat utilization rates, including off-label use, amongst females of reproductive potential (i.e., females aged 15 to 50 years) calculated cumulatively from the initial U.S. approval date annually through the 5th year following the initial U.S. approval date

L3128: ## 1. Background
L3129: In this submission the sponsor included reports of two animal carcinogenicity studies, one in rats and one in mice. These studies were to determine the carcinogenic potential of GSK1278863A, a HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, when given once daily by oral gavage for up to 104 consecutive weeks to Crl:CD (SD) rats, and once daily by oral gavage and subcutaneous injection of a cocktail formulation containing the three major circulating human metabolites for a minimum of 104 weeks to Crl:CD1 (ICR) mice, respectively.
L3130: In this review the phrase "dose response relationship" refers to the linear component (trend) of the effect of treatment, and not necessarily to a strictly increasing or decreasing mortality or tumor incidence rate as dose increases.
L3131: ## 2. Rat Study
L3132: Two separate experiments, one in male rats and one in female rats were conducted. As indicated in Table 1, in each of these two experiments there were four treated groups, and one vehicle control group. Three hundred and fifty Crl:CD (SD) rats of each sex were assigned randomly in size of 70 rats per group. The dose levels for the four treated groups were 0.02, 0.2, 0.8, and 4 mg/kg/day for male rats, and 0.02, 0.2, 0.8, and 7 mg/kg/day for female rats, respectively. In this review these dose groups were referred to as the low (Group 2), mid (Group 3), mid-high (Group 4), and high (Group 5) dose groups, respectively. The rats in the vehicle control groups were administrated with 1% (w/v) methyl cellulose (400 cP@ 2%) with 0.2% Tween 80 (v/v) with 5 mM NaOH in Ultra Pure Water, and handled for the same duration and in the same manner as the treated groups.
L3133: In view of the fact that the number of survivors had reached 15 in the high dose male rats (Group 5, 4 mg/kg/day) on Day 650, and had reached 20 in the Reference Item group on Days 675 and 695 for male and female rats, respectively, early study termination was initiated on Day 653 for Group 5 of male rats, Day 679 for Group 1 to Group 4 of male rats and on Day 698 for all female rats.

L3136: A viability check was performed near the start and end of each working day for main study animals. A necropsy was performed on those animals that died or were euthanized during the dosing period. Detailed examinations were performed on all Main Study animals weekly starting during the last week of the prestudy period and on the day of necropsy. All animals found dead during the study were subjected to necropsy, and tissue samples were preserved. Main study
L3137: animals were subjected to a complete necropsy examination, which included evaluation of the carcass and musculoskeletal system; all external surfaces and orifices; cranial cavity and external surfaces of the brain; and thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic cavities with their associated organs and tissues.
L3138: ## 2.1. Sponsor's analyses
L3139: ## 2.1.1. Survival analysis
L3140: In the sponsor's report, each animal survival time was measured by the number of study days until its death. The animal was classified as uncensored when death occurred within the experimental period and was not accidental. Otherwise, that is, when death was accidental, as it is the case for animals' nos. 3016 and 4524, and/or occurred during the terminal sacrifice period, the animal was classified as censored. The first day of the terminal sacrifice period was considered as the censoring time of all terminal animals.
L3141: For each sex, Kaplan-Meier product-limit method, applied on daily intervals, was used to estimate each group survival function for the dosing period and to generate the corresponding survival curves for males and females. At the 5% level, the significance of a dose-related trend in mortality across the reference item group (Group 1) and the four test item treated groups (Groups 2 to 5) was evaluated for each sex via Peto's two-sided test (Peto et al., 1980), using the corresponding arithmetic dose level scores. For the females, the doses are 0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.8, and 7 mg/kg/day. However, for the males, given that dosing stopped after Day 670 for Groups 1 to 4 and at Day 631 for Group 5, and given that the first day of sacrifice was Day 679 for Groups 1 to 4 and Day 653 for Group 5, the doses 0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.8, and 4 mg/kg/day were adjusted accordingly and, the adjusted doses 0, 0.0198, 0.0988, 0.7906, and 3.8712 mg/kg/day were used. In addition, Peto's two-tailed trend test was conducted, at the 5% significance level, to compare the mortality rates in the reference item group and in each of the test item treated group.
L3142: ## Sponsor's findings:
L3143: The sponsor's analysis showed that the numbers of rats surviving to their terminal necropsy were 20 (29%), 17 (24%), 17 (24%), 16 (23%), and 15 (21%) in the vehicle control, the low, mid, mid-high, and high dose groups for male rats, respectively, and 20 (29%), 21 (30%), 20 (29%), 27 (39%), and 30 (43%) for female rats respectively. For female rats, the trend and the pairwise comparisons test results were not found to be significant. For male rats, the trend test result revealed a significant increase in the mortality rate across doses, with p-value = 0.0025, and the pairwise comparison results revealed that the mortality rate in the high dose group (Group 5) is significantly higher than the one in the vehicle control group (Group 1), with p-value = 0.0131.
L3144: ## 2.1.2. Tumor data analysis
L3145: In the sponsor's analysis, the statistical evaluation was done for each sex separately and was limited to all non-secondary neoplastic lesions found in study plan-required tissues/sites as well as to the combined hemangiosarcomas across whole body. Tumors listed under subcutis and hemolymphoreticular tissue were statistically analyzed using all study animals. Tumors listed
L3146: under tissues/sites that were not systematically examined for all animals were excluded from the statistical analysis.
L3147: For male rats, given that the last day of dosing was Day 670 for Groups 1 to 4 and Day 631 for Group 5, and given that the first day of terminal sacrifice was Day 679 for animals in Groups 1 to 4 and Day 653 for animals in Group 5, two separate analyses were considered. More precisely, the first one included all groups with a common experimental period of 652 days and with doses 0, 0.02, 0.1, and 0.8 mg/kg/day for Groups 1 to 4 respectively, and adjusted dose of 3.8712 mg/kg/day for Group 5. The second analysis included Groups 1 to 4, with a common experimental period of 678 days and with respective adjusted doses of 0, 0.0198, 0.0988, and 0.7906 mg/kg/day. For female rats, given that animals in all groups have been dosed during the common experimental period of 697 days, only one analysis, with all groups and respective doses 0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.8, and 7 mg/kg/day, was conducted. In addition to the overall trend test, pairwise groups comparisons were made using Peto's one-sided test to determine if the tumor rate in each of the test item treated group is significantly higher than the one in the reference item group.
L3148: Neoplastic lesions designated as palpable and listed under clitoral, preputial and mammary glands, and under skin and subcutis were statistically analyzed according to Peto's onset rate method for tumors observed in a "mortality independent" context (Peto et al., 1980), using all animals. The onset time of each palpable tumor was given by the first date of detection. The death time was used as the onset time for a lesion categorized as palpable and not detected in-vivo. The death time of all animals dying after the end of the experimental period will be considered to be the first day following the experimental period.
L3149: For combinations of both palpable and non-palpable tumors, the animal death time was used in the analysis which was conducted according to the "mortality dependent" method described hereafter for non palpable tumors. Tumors categorized as non-palpable were analyzed using the "mortality dependent" method. In this context, each neoplastic finding was classified as the cause of death (designated by the study pathologist as definitely or probably fatal) or not the cause of death (designated by the study pathologist as definitely or probably incidental or undetermined). However, all non-palpable neoplasms found in an animal were automatically classified as incidental if the animal in question died after the experimental period. For combinations of neoplastic findings, if an animal had one of the related tumors classified as fatal, then the neoplastic finding defined by this combination was classified as fatal. Otherwise, it was classified as incidental. Neoplastic findings classified as fatal and incidental were processed using the death rate method and the prevalence method, respectively.
L3150: As per FDA's draft guidance (FDA's draft Guidance for industry, 2001), the processing of incidental tumors was done by creating a single separate interval for the scheduled terminal sacrifice period and by dividing the experimental period into the following fixed intervals: Days 0-350, Days 351-560, Days 561-652, and Day 653 and over for male rats first analysis, Days 0-350, Days 351-560, Days 561-678, and Day 679 and over for male rats second analysis, and Days 0-350, Days 351-560, Days 561-697, and Day 698 and over for female rats analysis.
L3151: Using the derived outcomes from the processing of both fatal and incidental tumors, a test statistic was built to perform a global survival-adjusted trend test on tumor data observed in a “mortality dependent” context (Peto et al., 1980). For each dataset of interest within each sex, the significance of a linear dose-related increase in tumor occurrence rates across the reference item group and test item treated groups was evaluated using Peto's survival-adjusted one-tailed trend test. The related arithmetic dose level scores, multiplied by 10 to the power 4 for male rats and 2 for female rats, were used to perform the overall trend test.
L3152: As mentioned by Lin (Lin, 1997), the discrete permutation distribution was used to compute the corresponding p-value for each statistical test performed on a dataset containing 10 or less tumor occurrences. The interpretation of the results should be accomplished with the consideration of both historical control data and biological relevance. In fact, the evaluation of the carcinogenic potential of the test item should be undertaken in the light of an overall scientific judgment.
L3153: ## Adjustment for multiple testing:
L3154: In the sponsor's report, according to the recommendations of Lin and Rahman (Lin and Rahman, 1998), the dose-related increase in tumor incidence should be considered significant if the p-value is less than or equal to 0.025 for rare tumors and less than or equal to 0.005 for common tumors (historical incidence of more than 1%); the increased tumor rate in a test item treated group when compared with the reference item group is considered to be significant when the p-value is less than or equal to 0.05 for a rare tumor, or is less than or equal to 0.01 for a common tumor.
L3155: ## Sponsor's findings:
L3156: In the sponsor's report, the overall trend results from the analysis of male rats data excluding Group 5, were not found to be significant (p\text{-value} &gt; 0.05), whereas the overall trend results from the analysis of male rats data and female rats data including all groups, revealed significance (p\text{-value} \le 0.05) for the datasets listed in Table 2.

L3166: ## 2.2. Reviewer's analyses
L3167: To verify the sponsor's analyses and to perform additional analyses suggested by the reviewing toxicologist, this reviewer independently performed the survival and tumor data analyses using the data provided by the sponsor electronically.
L3168: ## 2.2.1. Survival analysis
L3169: In the reviewer's analysis, the survival distributions of rats in all five groups (Groups 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier product limit method. The dose response relationship was tested across Groups 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 using the likelihood ratio test, and the homogeneity of survival distributions was tested using the log-rank test. The Kaplan-Meier curves for survival rates are
L3170: given in Figures 1A and 1B in the appendix for all five groups in male and female rats, respectively. The intercurrent mortality data of all five groups and the results of the tests for dose response relationship and homogeneity of survivals for Groups 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are given in Tables 1A and 1B in the appendix for male and female rats, respectively.
L3171: ## Reviewer's findings:
L3172: The reviewer's analysis showed that the numbers of rats surviving to their terminal necropsy were 20 (29%), 17 (24%), 17 (24%), 16 (23%), and 15 (21%) in the vehicle control, the low, mid, mid-high, and high dose groups for male rats, respectively, and 20 (29%), 21 (30%), 20 (29%), 27 (39%), and 30 (43%) for female rats respectively. A statistically significant increasing trend in mortality was noted for male rats (p-value = 0.0040), with a corresponding statistically significant increase in the high dose group when compared to the vehicle control group (p-values = 0.0143). No other statistically significant dose response relationship and pairwise comparisons in mortality was noted for male and female rats.
L3173: ## 2.2.2. Tumor data analysis
L3174: The tumor data were analyzed for dose response relationships across the vehicle control group, and low, mid, mid-high, and high dose groups, and pairwise comparisons of each of the four treated groups against the vehicle control group, using the Poly-k method described in the paper of Bailer and Portier (1988) and Bieler and Williams (1993).
L3175: In the poly-k method, the adjustment for differences in mortality among treatment groups is made by modifying the number of animals at risk in the denominators in the calculations of overall tumor rates in the Cochran-Armitage test to reflect less-than-whole-animal contributions for animals that die without tumor before the end of the study (Bailer and Portier 1988). The modification is made by defining a new number of animals at risk for each treatment group. The number of animals at risk for the i-th treatment group R^*_i is defined as R^*_i = \sum W_{ij} where w_{ij} is the weight for the j-th animal in the i-th treatment group, and the sum is over all animals in the group.
L3176: Bailer and Portier (1988) proposed the weight w_{ij} as follows:
L3177: w_{ij} = 1 to animals dying with the tumor, and
L3178: w_{ij} = (t_{ij} / t_{sacr})^3 to animals dying without the tumor,
L3179: where t_{ij} is the time of death of the j-th animal in the i-th treatment group, and t_{sacr} is the planned (or intended) time of terminal sacrifice. The above formulas imply that animals living up to the end of the planned terminal sacrifice date without developing any tumor will also be assigned w_{ij} = 1 since t_{ij} = t_{sacr}. Also animals developed the tumor type being tested before the end of the study will be assigned as w_{ij} = 1.
L3180: Certain treatment groups of a study or the entire study may be terminated earlier than the planned (or intended) time of terminal sacrifice due to excessive mortalities. However, based on the principle of the Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis in randomized trials, the t_{sacr} should not be affected by the unplanned early terminations. The t_{sacr} should always be equal to the planned (or intended) time of terminal sacrifice. For those animals that were sacrificed later than t_{sacr},
L3181: regardless their actual terminal sacrifice time, tsacr was used as their time of terminal sacrifice in the analysis.
L3182: One critical point for Poly-k test is the choice of the appropriate value of k, which depends on the tumor incidence pattern with the increased dose. For long term 104 week standard rat and mouse studies, a value of k=3 is suggested in the literature. Hence, this reviewer used k=3 for the analysis of this data.
L3183: ## **Multiple testing adjustment:**
L3184: For the adjustment of multiple testing, this reviewer used the methodologies suggested in the FDA guidance for statistical design and analysis of carcinogenicity studies (2001). For dose response relationship tests, the guidance suggests the use of test levels of \alpha=0.005 for common tumors and \alpha=0.025 for rare tumors for a submission with two species where both are two-years studies, in order to keep the false-positive rate at the nominal level of approximately 10%. For multiple pairwise comparisons of treated group with control, the guidance suggests the use of test levels of \alpha=0.01 for common tumors and \alpha=0.05 for rare tumors, in order to keep the false-positive rate at the nominal level of approximately 10% for both submissions with two or one species.
L3185: A rare tumor is defined as one in which the published spontaneous tumor rate is less than 1%. However, if the background information for the common or rare tumor is not available, the number of animals bearing tumors in the vehicle control group in the present study was used to determine the common or rare tumor status in the review report.
L3186: ## **Reviewer's findings:**
L3187: The tumor rates and the p-values of the tested tumor types are listed in Tables 2A and 2B in the appendix for male and female rats, respectively. The tumor types with p-values less than or equal to 0.05 for dose response relationship and/or pairwise comparisons of treated groups and vehicle control are reported in Table 4.
L3188: Based on the criteria of adjustment for multiple testing discussed above, for male rats, a statistically significant dose response relationship was noted in the incidence of fibroadenoma in mammary gland (p-value = 0.0005), with a corresponding statistically significant increase in the high dose group (Group 5) when compared to the vehicle control group (p-value = 0.0044), regardless of the tumor classification (rare or common). Statistically significant dose response relationships were also noted in the incidence of hemangiosarcoma in spleen, and adenoma in stomach (p-value = 0.0224 and 0.0224, respectively) without corresponding statistically significant pairwise comparisons if these tumors were considered to be rare tumors. No statistically significant findings were noted in tumor data for female rats.

L3194: ## 3. Mouse Study
L3195: Two separate experiments, one in male mice and one in female mice were conducted. As indicated in Table 5, in the experiment there were four treated groups, and one vehicle control group. Three hundred Crl:CD1 (ICR) mice of each sex, respectively, were assigned randomly in size of 60 mice per group. Three of the four treated groups received once daily oral gavage at 0.2, 0.8, or 3 mg/kg/day of GSK1278863 for a minimum of 104 weeks for both male and female mice. These three treated groups were also dosed via once daily subcutaneous injection of a cocktail formulation containing the three major circulating human metabolites [2.0 mg/kg/day GSK2391220 (M2), 2.5 mg/kg/day GSK2506104 (M3) and 1.3 mg/kg/day GSK2531401 (M13)]. In this review these three treated groups were referred to as the low (Group 2), mid (Group 4), and high (Group 5) dose groups, respectively. The other treated group (Group 3) received 0.8 mg/kg/day GSK1278863 by once daily oral gavage + subcutaneous reference item by once daily subcutaneous injection without metabolites. The mice in the vehicle control group (Group 1) were administrated once daily with oral gavage at 0 mg/kg/day of GSK1278863 and subcutaneous reference items [1% (w/v) methyl cellulose (400 cP@ 2%) / 0.2% Tween 80 (v/v) / 5 mM NaOH in Ultra Pure Water], and handled for the same duration and in the same manner as the treated groups.
L3196: The same clinical examinations, laboratory investigations and pathology procedures used in the rat study were performed in the mouse study.

L3200: ## 3.1. Sponsor's analyses
L3201: ## 3.1.1. Survival analysis
L3202: In the sponsor's report, each animal survival time was measured by the number of study days until its death. The animal was classified as uncensored when death occurred within the experimental period and was not accidental. Otherwise, that is, when death was accidental, as it is the case for Animal No. 2532, and/or whenever death occurred during the terminal sacrifice period, the animal was classified as censored. The first day of the terminal sacrifice period, Day 729, was considered as the censoring time of all terminal animals.
L3203: For each sex, Kaplan-Meier product-limit method, applied on daily intervals, was used to estimate each group survival function for the dosing period, and to generate the corresponding survival curves. At the 5% level, the significance of an overall dose-related trend in mortality across the reference item group (Group 1) and the three test item treated groups having the same subcutaneous dose level (Groups 2, 4, and 5) was evaluated for each sex via Peto's two-sided test (Peto et al., 1980), using the corresponding oral dose level scores 0, 0.2, 0.8, and 3 mg/kg/day. In addition, Peto's two-tailed test was conducted, at the 5% significance level, to compare the mortality rates in the reference item group and in each of Groups 2, 4, and 5.
L3204: ## Sponsor's findings:
L3205: The sponsor's analysis showed that the numbers of mice surviving to their terminal necropsy were 34 (57%), 33 (55%), 28 (47%), 33 (55%), and 32 (53%) in the vehicle control group, the low, mid, and high dose groups, and Group 3 for male mice, respectively, and 29 (48%), 27 (45%), 36 (60%), 26 (43%), and 32 (53%) for female mice respectively. No statistically significant findings in mortality were noted for both male and female mice.
L3206: ## 3.1.2. Tumor data analysis
L3207: Regarding the tumor data, the statistical evaluation was done for each sex separately and was limited to all non-secondary neoplastic lesions found in study plan-required tissues/sites as well as to the combined hemangiosarcomas across whole body. Tumors listed under subcutis and hemolymphoreticular tissue were statistically analyzed using all study animals.
L3208: Neoplastic lesions designated as palpable and listed under mammary glands, skin and subcutis were statistically analyzed according to Peto's onset rate method for tumors observed in a "mortality independent" context (Peto et al., 1980), using all animals. The onset time of each palpable tumor was given by the first date of detection. The death time was used as the onset time for a lesion categorized as palpable and not detected invivo. The death time of all animals dying after the end of the experimental period will be considered to be the first day following the experimental period. For combinations of both palpable and non-palpable tumors, the animal death time was used in the analysis which was conducted according to the "mortality dependent" method described hereafter for non palpable tumors. Tumors categorized as non-palpable were analyzed using the "mortality dependent" method. In this context, each neoplastic finding was classified as the cause of death (designated by the study pathologist as definitely or probably fatal) or not the cause of death (designated by the study pathologist as definitely or probably incidental or undetermined). However, all non-palpable neoplasms found in an animal were automatically classified as incidental if the animal in question died after the experimental period. For combinations of neoplastic findings, if an animal had one of the related tumors classified as fatal, then the neoplastic finding defined by this combination was classified as fatal. Otherwise, it was classified as incidental.
L3209: Neoplastic findings classified as fatal and incidental were processed using the death rate method and the prevalence method, respectively. As per FDA's draft guidance (FDA's draft Guidance for industry, 2001), the processing of incidental tumors was done by creating a single separate interval for the scheduled terminal sacrifice period and by dividing the experimental period into the following fixed intervals: Days 0-364, Days 365-546, Days 547-644, and Days 645-728. Using the derived outcomes from the processing of both fatal and incidental tumors, a test statistic was built to perform a global survival-adjusted trend test on tumor data observed in a "mortality dependent" context (Peto et al., 1980). For each dataset of interest within each sex, the significance of a linear dose-related increase in tumor occurrence rates across Groups 1, 2, 4, and 5 was evaluated using Peto's survival-adjusted one-tailed trend test. For both sexes, the related oral dose level scores multiplied by 10 were used to perform the overall trend test. In addition to the overall trend test, pairwise group comparisons were made using Peto's one-sided test to determine if the tumor rate in each of Groups 2, 4, and 5 were significantly higher than the one in Group 1.
L3210: As mentioned by Lin (Lin, 1997), the discrete permutation distribution was used to compute the corresponding p-value for each statistical test performed on a dataset containing 10 or less tumor occurrences. The interpretation of the results should be accomplished with the consideration of both historical control data and biological relevance. In fact, the evaluation of the carcinogenic potential of the test item should be undertaken in the light of an overall scientific judgment.
L3211: ## **Multiple testing adjustment:**
L3212: According to the recommendations of Lin and Rahman (Lin and Rahman, 1998), the dose-related increase in tumor incidence should be considered significant if the p-value is less than or equal to 0.025 for rare tumors and less than or equal to 0.005 for common tumors (historical incidence of more than 1%); the increased tumor rate in a test item treated group when compared
L3213: with the reference item group is considered to be significant when the p-value is less than or equal to 0.05 for a rare tumor, or is less than or equal to 0.01 for a common tumor.
L3214: ## Sponsor's findings:
L3215: In the sponsor's report, based on the adjustment criteria for multiple testing described in the sponsor's report, no statistically significant overall trend was noted in tumor data for both male and female mice. The pairwise comparison results revealed significance (p\text{-value} \le 0.05) for the datasets listed in Table 6.
